articles.title: UK court convicts 2 Iranian men of spying on journalists
articles.summary: A London court has found two Iranian citizens guilty of surveilling reporters for a Persian-language television station critical of Iran's goverment. One was also convicted of planning a violent…

image.caption: The trial opened at Woolwich Crown Court in London on October 5 this yearImage: Kin Cheung/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Two Iranian men were found guilty of spying in dissident journalists in Britain on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guard on Thursday.

British counterterrorism police said the case reflected intensifying hostile Iranian activity in the country, an issue that recently made headlines amid the security scare at the RAF Fairford airbase that's a major operational site in Europe for the US Air Force.
The men, both in their 40s, were arrested last year, with Iran repeatedly rejecting the allegations against them.
What did the court rule?

The Woolwich Crown Court in London convicted one of the Iranian citizens not just of spying on journalists working for the Persian-language dissident TV channel Iran International, but of plotting a violent attack against one or more of them.
The second individual had also faced charges of plotting an attack but was only convicted of spying on the reporters.
One of the convicted defendants said he was acting under duress after his family was threatened, and the other said he did not know that his actions were assisting Iranian intelligence.
A third defendant, a 57-year-old Iranian man, was acquitted of all charges.

blocks.caption: Sentencing in the case is expected at the 'Old Bailey' in London on December 17Image: Kin Cheung/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The men were accused of engaging in conduct likely to assist the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Iran's multi-discipline military force that's seen as closer to the country's religious leadership and more influential than its regular armed forces.

The UK formally designated the IRGC as a threat to national security in July, meaning that supporting or assisting the organization can carry penalties of up to 14 years in prison as part of new rules on national security and state threats.
Sentencing in this case is still pending and is scheduled for mid-December.

"This was a calculated operation to spy on those critical of the Iranian regime," said Frank Ferguson, chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service's special crime and counter-terrorism division.
The two men were accused of visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos and videos, and using platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online
"Thankfully, the defendants were stopped before any attack could take place," prosecutor Ferguson said.
Senior ‌National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said that the IRGC or "middlemen" for Iranian intelligence were directing the plot.
Iran's government had repeatedly denied the allegations, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi saying he was "disturbed" by the trio's arrests last May.
UK releases air base plot suspects
Not the first plot targeting Iran International
There have been four cases targeting the Persian language television channel Iran International since late 2023.
In July, two Romanian men were jailed for stabbing a journalist outside his home in 2024.

A spokesman for the broadcaster's parent company, Volant Media, said in a statement that Thursday's verdicts "don't make the lives of our journalists any safer so long as the Islamic Republic of Iran continues its campaign of death threats and violence against them."
Iran International reported that a British barrister was also one of the targets.
What other alleged signs of Iranian hostile activity in the UK are there?
British law enforcement has been warning of an uptick of hostile Iranian activity in recent years, particularly since the US military operations against Tehran began earlier this year.

Most notably, the UK has accused Iran of being behind a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford base in September, after which US President Donald Trump withdrew some long-range bombers from the site.
Three men were indicted in the US in relation that plot this week, while two others currently face charges in the UK.

But beyond this, the head of Britain's MI5 domestic intelligence agency Ken MacCullum said in October that Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests in the last year. He also said known cases of so-called state threats had more than quadrupled in a decade.
Counter-terrorism police chief Evans said she expected this trend to continue.
France this week also accused Iran of being behind a cyberattack targeting refrigeration units at hundreds of supermarkets in October, although Iran denied any involvement.

European governments are on heightened alert for so-called hybrid warfare tactics, from Russia as well as Iran, amid the geopolitical tensions of recent years. New technologies like low-cost drones and AI are also threatening to make such activities cheaper, harder to trace, and potentially more effective.

articles.title: Impeachment: How it works and why Trump should be worried
articles.summary: Pete Hegseth, Bill Clinton and Donald Trump (twice so far): attempts to impeach political figures are becoming common. The failure rate looks high, but according to experts, conviction is not always…

image.caption: Donald Trump and Pete Hegseth have both been impeached but neither was forced outImage: Evelyn Hockstein/REUTERS

blocks.text: Pete Hegseth, US President Donald Trump's secretary of war, described the failed efforts to impeach him this week as "farce" and "sabotage".

The case, built on an accusation that Hegseth waged war on Iran without the proper congressional approval, always looked a long shot. But many observers believe it could be the first in a wave of impeachment attempts, possibly headlined by a third attempt to impeach Trump.
DW takes a look at impeachments and why you may be hearing more about them.

While there are global variations in how impeachment works, in the US it is a process that allows the legislature (usually Congress, state or tribal legislature) to bring charges against an elected figure — a judge or a president, for example. These are not criminal charges but can result in the removal of the accused party from their post.

For federal impeachment, once an impeachment case is raised in the House of Representatives, it must be heard in a trial in the Senate, with both sides able to cross-examine relevant figures. However, for a conviction to be obtained, a two-thirds majority must be reached, a factor which often limits the chances of success given the partisan nature of US politics.
It is a simple process to introduce and, once started, the case is heard within 48 hours, as was the case with Hegseth.
What is impeachment used for in US politics?

Given only eight people, all judges, have been impeached since the first case concluded in 1799, the odds of impeaching a high-level politician are long. The two-thirds majority rule has meant that impeachment is instead often used to draw attention to perceived misdemeanors and potentially force a resignation.

"Using impeachment threats as a signaling device is a fairly old tactic, but it has certainly become more common in the Trump-[Joe] Biden era," Frank O Bowman III, a law professor at the University of Missouri and author of a forthcoming book on impeachment and Donald Trump, told DW.
That, added Keith Whittingtona Yale Law School professor and impeachment expert, was not what impeachment was intended to do.

blocks.caption: Democratic President, Bill Clinton, was acquitted of lying under oath in 1999Image: J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Congress has tended to take an extremely partisan approach to making use of the power. That has doomed any possibility of conviction and removal," he told DW.

"The possibility of partisan use of the impeachment power became evident very quickly in American history, but the founders certainly would not have intended or hoped that the impeachment power would be used as a partisan weapon or a means of partisan messaging."
Will Donald Trump be a target for impeachment for a third time?

The recent midterm results will see the Democrats control both houses of Congress from next year, meaning there is a greater chance that the US President could be impeached for an unprecedented third time. He was acquitted on "charges of abuse of power and obstruction of Congress" in 2020 and then on the charge of "incitement of insurrection" in 2021.

Bowman consulted in both cases. "In my view, they should have succeeded," he said. "But they didn't and, from the perspective of the average member of the public, it's just fuss and bother, but nothing happened. So why are we even bothering? I do think that in the public mind, impeachment has been significantly devalued."

The law expert said there are multiple ways Congress could try again, including "conduct that rises to the level of treason, bribery, other high crimes or misuse," but political considerations are critical.

"Democrats should not start out their control of the House by rushing off to impeach Trump because … it would detract from what I think they need to be doing. That is demonstrating to the public that, having regained control of the legislature, they're at least going to try to do things which are of practical importance to the average person."
What will Democrats do with their midterm mandate?

However, given the midterm results, Bowman thinks there is a chance that if enough Republicans — and public sentiment — turn further against Trump, the numbers could work. Should that time come, added Whittington, there is one particular avenue open to the Democrats.

"The best strategy would be close negotiations with Republican senators to discover if there are any grounds that might peel off the votes that they would need from across the aisle," Whittington said. "That might not be very satisfactory for the Democratic base, but that would put the president at greatest risk of conviction and removal."
What about other members of the Trump administration?
The Hegseth case, effectively killed after the House of Representatives voted to refer impeachment articles to a committee, shows an appetite for impeachment against members of Trump's cabinet.

Indeed, impeachment resolutions have already been filed against Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Education Secretary Linda McMahon, and Attorney General Todd Blanche could also be in the sights of Democrats in the upcoming Congress.

blocks.caption: US Attorney General Todd Blanche, who has warned US Democrats against investigating Trump administration officials, could also be a target for impeachmentImage: Bonnie Cash/UPI Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: "The Democrats will face a tremendous amount of pressure from their own base to consider impeachments, and the fact that so many Democrats in the House supported the Hegseth impeachment in this procedural vote suggests that there will be an appetite to pursue that possibility in the next Congress," said Whittington.
With getting the votes to impeach Trump perhaps tougher due to his "cult of personality” within the Republican party, picking off his closest allies may be in play, said Bowman.

"You could eliminate cabinet officers, as a means of making a point to the administration, that: 'OK, we're not going to come after the big man himself, but if the rest of you minions insist on doing bad stuff, we will take you out.'"
Why do so few impeachment cases seem to fail?

Essentially, this is down to the two-thirds majority rule, according to both experts. Given that neither party has enjoyed such a majority since the mid 1960s, any conviction requires significant support from opponents.
But, actually, said Whittington, a conviction is not the only way to judge the success of an impeachment.
"Often the impeachment threat is itself sufficient to encourage an officer mired in scandal to resign, so that an actual conviction at trial is not necessary," he said

"Impeachment trials are more rare than they might otherwise be simply because impeachment threats are often successful. But, of course, some officers are willing to ride an impeachment out and take their chances at trial."

blocks.text: Multiple people shot after incident in Washington DC, say police

blocks.caption: Anna Betts

blocks.text: Anna Betts
Multiple people have been shot in north-west Washington DC on Thursday morning, local police have confirmed, prompting a “barricade situation” in the area.
In a statement at 9.21am ET, the DC police said that the incident has “resulted in a barricade situation in the 1500 block of 15th Street, Northwest”.
“Please avoid the area as we work to resolve the incident,” they added.

A Vida Fitness manager told ABC7News that shots were fired outside the business. The local news station reported that as of 9am local time on Thursday morning, the business was still under lockdown and there is police inside the building.
The manager said that they feel safe with police inside, and that the gym will be closed the rest of the day.
Several schools in the area are on lockdown on Thursday morning.
Key events

items: 36m agoMultiple people shot after incident in Washington DC, say police
44m agoPolice issue shelter-in-place order after at least five people shot in Logan Circle neighborhood of Washington DC

blocks.text: District of Columbia Public Schools has put multiple schools in the vicinity of the shooting on alert status, meaning no one can go in or out of the campuses, but activities inside remain normal.
A post on social media reported that a nearby building appeared to be on fire. The Guardian has not been able to independently verify this claim.
James Spellman was at the gym a little after 8am when he heard shots being fired. He said there were about 50 people in the gym at the time, reported AP.
“Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out,” he said. “One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck.”

Spellman told AP that he and other gym members ran out of the gym, and he said he heard more gunfire in the area of 15th Street. He said he heard about two shots fired in the gym and about five or six fired outside.
Witness Ryan Dubicki was in his nearby apartment around 8 am when, he said, he “heard about five bangs.”
“They were really spread out so I thought it was construction,” he said. It was only a short time later that he looked out “and there were cops everywhere.”
His apartment building managers sent a notice that there was a possible active shooter, reported AP.
Gun violence charity March for Our Lives wrote about the incident online, saying:

double quotation markJust after 8AM, a gunman opened fire at the VIDA Fitness in Logan Circle, right here in Washington, DC. At least five people were shot, the surrounding blocks were locked down, and nearby schools were put on alert. People who walked in for a morning workout found themselves running for their lives and sheltering from gunfire. What should have been an ordinary Thursday morning became a scene none of our neighbors should ever have to carry. This is why we do this work. Gun violence doesn’t just happen somewhere else. Today it happened down the street, and we will not accept it as normal.
The shootings were reported in Logan Circle, about 1 mile north of the White House.

Police urged people to avoid the area of the 1500 block of 15th Street, which includes a VIDA fitness center, St. Luke’s Episcopal Church and residences and is around the corner from a Whole Foods supermarket, the AP reports.
Much of the block was cordoned off. Schools near the scene were placed on lockdown.
Armed police and members of the National Guard were visible around the Logan Circle area of Washington DC after the incident began on Thursday morning.

blocks.caption: Armed police on a rooftop as they respond to a shooting in Logan Circle, Washington DC. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
Members of the National Guard near the scene of the shooting in Logan Circle, Washington DC. Photograph: Ken Cedeno/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Police issue shelter-in-place order after at least five people shot in Logan Circle neighborhood of Washington DC
At least five people have been shot in Northwest Washington DC on Thursday morning, local police confirmed to the Associated Press.
A spokesperson for the Washington DC police department told the Guardian in a brief phone call on Thursday morning that the scene was “still active”. No further details were immediately available.

The DC police department said in a social media post at about 8.20am ET that officers were on the scene responding to an “active shooting in the area of 15th and P Street, Northwest”. The department’s emergency response team was also at the scene. The department urged the public to avoid the area.

The Metropolitan police department has also issued a shelter-in-place order for those in the immediate vicinity of the 1500 block of 15th Street NW. They have urged residents to “go inside to the nearest building, stay away from windows and remain indoors until further notice”.
Local council member Brooke Pinto also posted on social media on Thursday morning that there had been a shooting “at and outside Vida fitness this morning in Logan Circle”.
“Do not go to this area,” Pinto said. “Police looking for suspect.”
A reporter for the Washington Sun said that they spoke with a witness who was in the gym and “heard one gunshot and saw one person down in the gym itself, followed by more shots”.
The person told the reporter that the gym “cleared out” and that people were running from the scene with their “arms raised” as police yelled to clear out.

articles.title: Jensen Huang: Spy row, second affair leaves Nvidia without its rockstar CEO
articles.summary: Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia into the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, is stepping down as CEO after a second affair came to light. DW examines how losing its figurehead will affect the firm and the…

image.caption: Jensen Huang started Nvidia in 1993, aged 30Image: Lisi Niesner/REUTERS

blocks.text: 1. What do we know about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure?
Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future after reports emerged of a second extramarital affair — this time with an employee.
In a statement issued on Thursday morning, the world's most valuable chip supplier said Huang was resigning as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately.
The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.
Under Nvidia's bylaws, Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of its 11 directors.
The New York Times first reported on the latest scandal, alleging that the 63-year-old Huang had an affair a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.
Both are married; Huang tied the knot with his wife Lori in 1985.
The latest revelation emerged just three days after Huang admitted a relationship with a Chinese woman, whom United States intelligence agencies believe was spying for China.
The woman, Alice H., is an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that runs artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across Southeast Asia and is a major client of Nvidia.
The US government is investigating the startup on suspicion that it secretly sent some of its Nvidia chips to China, violating Washington's curbs on high-end semiconductors.
Those advanced Nvidia processors ‌are ​used to train and run the large AI models behind chatbots and other generative AI products.
Megaspeed denies the allegations and on Thursday pledged to cooperate with US investigators. H., the alleged spy, has been barred from entering Singapore and Taiwan — a key chipmaking island.
While Nvidia's board backed its CEO after the first scandal emerged, market watchers believe the second caused too much reputational damage to one of the world's top three companies by market value.

blocks.caption: Nvidia is the hardware backbone of the global AI raceImage: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: 2. Who could replace Huang as Nvidia CEO?
According to The Wall Street Journal, Huang doesn't believe in formal succession planning, so with little notice, Nvidia appointed CFO Kress as interim CEO.
Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board is working with advisers to identify potential permanent successors.

Kress, other senior Nvidia executives and members of Huang's own family have been mooted as replacements. The family members include his daughter Madison, a senior director of product marketing, and his son Spencer, who currently works in the firm's robotics division.
Rumors also abound over a longer-term solution. On India's CNBC-TV18, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld from the Yale School of Management floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt.
Anthropic seeks $1.3 trillion valuation amid AI bubble fears
3. What will be the impact of Huang's departure on Nvidia?

The scandals have certainly hit Nvidia's market value. Since the first extramarital affair emerged on Sunday, the chipmaker's market capitalization has fallen by well over $600 billion to $4.2 trillion.
Nvidia shares were down more than 9% in premarket trading Thursday, after dropping by 10% earlier this week. Some analysts expect the stock price to struggle in the short term.

Nvidia stock hit all-time highs just a month ago as US technology giants continued to announce billions in spending on AI infrastructure. Still, Nvidia's stock hit all-time highs only a month ago, as US technology giants kept announcing billions in spending on AI infrastructure. Demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales. — meaning demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales.

"While Jensen [Huang] is the heart and lungs of the Nvidia story…the company and its leading-edge GPU technology will go on and [his departure] does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the fAI Revolution chip arms race," said Dan Ives, a partner, senior managing director and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, a US-based merchant bank
Analysts see the biggest long-term risk in strategy and execution. After all, Huang was the leader who picked which ideas Nvidia should bet heavily on and got the whole company behind them.
His sudden exit is also seen as highly disruptive to the chip designer's strong relationships with AI hyperscalers, Taiwanese chip producer TSMC and foreign governments — especially China.
Huang was Nvidia's main lobbyist on US chip export rules and persuaded US President Donald Trump to ease some curbs on China last year.

blocks.caption: NVIDIA's systemic position as an AI leader will help the post-Huang eraImage: Jens Kalaene/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: 4. How dangerous is it for firms like Nvidia to rely on so-called rockstar CEOs?
Huang is often called a rockstar CEO for his leather jackets instead of suits.
Like Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, he was also seen as a key-person risk as Nvidia’s public image, strategic direction and technical decisions became closely tied to him.
Huang steered the company for more than three decades and was also respected for his hands-on involvement in product architecture and engineering decisions.
He also insisted on a flat management structure, with around 60 executives reporting directly to him.
Huang has run the company so tightly around his own technical judgment and product decisions that investors may have little sense of how it would function without him.

At the same time, Nvidia is no longer the startup Huang founded in 1993. The company has built deep expertise in chip design and software, creating a durable moat that helps protect its huge profits, which topped $120.1 billion last year.
Some analysts argue that its central role in the AI hardware buildout makes it less dependent on Huang’s day-to-day input.
5. How will Huang's departure affect the US-China AI war?
China is quickly playing catch-up with the US in the global race for AI dominance.

While Chinese AI models have lagged behind the likes of ChatGPT and Claude, recent updates from DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot have closed much of the gap on benchmark tests and often beat US rivals on cost and speed.
Beijing is also investing heavily in domestic chips and data centers to reduce reliance on US hardware.
The US has curbed exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips.
However, this move has only slowed the pace of China's AI ambitions.

Reuters reported Thursday that Chinese AI firms are now trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China, amid fears the US could further tighten restrictions on advanced chips.
Also Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using the Nvidia spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade" on China.
The issue is likely to dominate talks next week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen in southern China.

articles.title: Senator opens investigation into evidence RFK Jr ‘unlawfully lied’ to Congress
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Ron Wyden, citing Guardian report, is launching inquiry into whether health secretary lied about Samoa trip during confirmation hearings

A top Democratic senator has launched an…

blocks.text: A top Democratic senator has launched an investigation into evidence that Robert F Kennedy Jr “unlawfully lied” in his 2025 confirmation hearings to become the US health secretary, citing a report by the Guardian.

Ron Wyden of Oregon, the incoming chair of the powerful Senate finance committee, is seeking extensive records from Children’s Health Defense (CHD), the non-profit anti-vaccine group Kennedy has used as a vehicle to fuel his political rise, including all documents related to a 2019 trip Kennedy took to Samoa.

“We are beginning an investigation into evidence that Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F Kennedy, Jr unlawfully lied to Congress on multiple occasions,” Wyden said in a letter to the group that was sent on Wednesday and obtained by the Guardian. The letter was also signed by Angela Alsobrooks, a Democratic senator from Maryland.

In the letter, the two lawmakers cited reporting by the Guardian that indicated Kennedy lied about his reasons for going to Samoa in 2019, a trip that occurred just months before a measles outbreak killed 83 people in the Pacific island nation, mostly children under age five.

The trip, which Kennedy made as the chair and chief legal counsel of CHD, became one of the most criticized events in his career before he entered government. Critics, including Samoan officials, have said Kennedy’s presence emboldened anti-vaccine activists in Samoa, worsening a vaccination crisis. Kennedy has denied the allegations, saying he never gave any public statement about vaccines or discouraged Samoans from getting vaccinated.

blocks.caption: The Samoan prime minister, Tuilaepa Sailele Malielegaoi, shakes hands with Robert F Kennedy Jr in Mulinu’u, Samoa, on 1 June 2019. Photograph: Misiona Simo/AP

blocks.text: “We are deeply concerned by the tactics Kennedy has used – both before and during his tenure as secretary – to stand in the way of children receiving life-saving vaccinations,” the two Democratic senators wrote. “In Samoa and in the United States, unvaccinated children have died tragic and preventable deaths during measles outbreaks. We intend to hold Secretary Kennedy accountable for the grave harm he has caused to vulnerable children. We also intend to hold him accountable for any false statements made to Congress, a crime that undermines the Senate’s ability to fulfill its constitutional duties.”
In two congressional confirmation hearings in January 2025, Kennedy told lawmakers who held the key to his confirmation that his visit to Samoa had “nothing to do with vaccines”.

But letters obtained by the Guardian and the Associated Press through an open records lawsuit brought by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press contradicted that testimony. In one he wrote to the Samoan prime minister in January 2019 before the trip, Kennedy explicitly said he wanted to study the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine in the Pacific island nation. In it, he used the words “vaccine” or “vaccination” eight times.
The prime minister responded a month later, saying Samoa could benefit from CHD’s assessment of MMR vaccines and inviting him to come.
Children’s Health Defense did not respond to requests for comment, and the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) did not immediately comment.

HHS previously said in response to the Guardian’s reporting on Kennedy’s Senate testimony that his visit to Samoa was “unrelated to vaccines. Any claim or insinuation based on these letters that Secretary Kennedy lied under oath or to Congress is not only false but outright defamatory.” It has not provided a response to questions about why his testimony contradicted what he said in his letter to the Samoan prime minister.

By requesting documents from CHD, Wyden is aiming at the heart of Kennedy’s political machine. Since taking office, Kennedy has hired former CHD employees, including Lyn Redwood, a former CHD president who made early outreach on his behalf to Samoa. Redwood is now an employee at the HHS, reportedly working on vaccine safety. Kennedy’s closest adviser at HHS, Stefanie Spear, ran CHD’s newsletter before joining his 2024 presidential campaign.

With Kennedy now in government, CHD and its leaders often act as his most vociferous defenders, praising his work and explaining his decisions on their video podcasts, articles and on social media. Kennedy headlined CHD’s annual conference in September, where he made false and misleading claims about the safety of vaccines.

The Senate letter requested all documents related to any travel to Samoa by Kennedy or other employees or associates of CHD and any communications with Samoan government officials. It also asked for records related to Kennedy’s presidential campaign and his Senate confirmation process.
In addition, the senators requested records related to Kennedy’s speech to CHD’s September convention and all communications between CHD and federal government officials since 20 January 2025.
CHD has a deadline of 4 December.

blocks.caption: Ron Wyden speaks at a Senate finance committee hearing on Capitol Hill on 22 July 2026. Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/Reuters

blocks.text: On the night of the election, after polls closed and it became clear Democrats would take a majority of seats in the Senate, Wyden made a social media post with a direct message about accountability. “Subpoenas,” he wrote, in the one-word post. Alsobrooks, a member of the Senate committee on health, education, labor and pensions, has repeatedly called on Kennedy to resign or be fired.

The letter does not go as far as the legal force of a subpoena. But it would be a good idea to treat such a letter seriously, said Tim Stretton, of the Project on Government Oversight, a nonpartisan watchdog group in Washington.
“It’s not wise to ignore it,” Stretton said. “It’s really in their interest now to cooperate in a good faith effort.”
If they don’t, he said, the committee or chair could issue subpoenas to demand the information they are seeking.
Knowingly giving material false testimony to Congress is a crime that carries a possible prison sentence, though it is rarely prosecuted.

Wyden previously called for a criminal investigation of Kennedy’s testimony about his trip to Samoa. He said in August he would be pressing Republican colleagues to issue a criminal referral of Kennedy to the Department of Justice for a criminal investigation. He said then that “when Democrats retake the majority in the Senate, RFK will be at the top of the list of Trump officials the finance committee will hold accountable for endangering American families”.

Several other Democrats have called for Kennedy to resign or be impeached. Bernie Sanders, incoming chair of the Senate committee on health, education, labor and pensions, said he is open to impeachment. And the incoming senator Annie Andrews, a pediatrician from South Carolina, has been calling for Kennedy’s impeachment since her campaign.

Legal experts have said it is unlikely the justice department under Trump would prosecute, but said Kennedy’s statements could be used as grounds for hearings, for an impeachment inquiry or to create other obstacles for the Trump administration.

articles.title: World leaders set out clashing priorities as COP31 turns to negotiations
articles.summary: Developing countries reiterate requests that they have made during many years of UN talks for rich countries to provide more finance to help them shift to cleaner energy, adapt to a warming world,…

blocks.text: LIGHTS ON. A drone light show displays the COP31 logo during the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, on November 11, 2026.
Kaan Soyturk/Reuters

Developing countries reiterate requests that they have made during many years of UN talks for rich countries to provide more finance to help them shift to cleaner energy, adapt to a warming world, and repair climate-driven destruction

items: World leaders at COP31 are presenting conflicting demands on climate action, complicating negotiations for a unified agreement.
Small island nations are urging immediate emission cuts, while European leaders support electrification and developing countries seek financial aid from wealthier nations.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

ANTALYA, Turkey – World leaders have set out competing positions and made clashing demands in two days of intense speech-making at the COP31 climate change talks in Turkey, leaving negotiators with a tough task to draft a meaningful deal that all can agree.
Small island states, among the most vulnerable in the world as global warming makes sea levels rise, pleaded for urgent cuts to greenhouse gas emissions.

European leaders, meanwhile, lined up behind a proposal to expand global electrification, developing countries asked for more finance from rich ones, and fossil fuel producers said oil, gas, and coal should continue to be used.

“We reaffirm our sovereign right to strengthen our energy and oil industry as a driver of our national development,” Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodriguez told the conference, after UN leaders had made the case for bringing to an end the age of fossil fuel.

Apart from trying to accommodate incompatible national positions aired on Wednesday, November 11 and Thursday, November 12, conference host Turkey and negotiations lead Australia also have the challenge of trying to make progress when wars and inflation have pushed climate concerns down the political agenda.

“It’s my job to steer consensus, not to bang tables and demand any particular action, but to steer consensus to the strongest, most ambitious possible outcome within the constraints of that consensus-driven process,” Chris Bowen, Australia’s COP31 president of negotiations, told Reuters.
Asked what a good deal might look like, he said: “I have many more hours of consultations with partners to do.”
Climate activists say short-term political concerns should not get in the way of addressing an issue that will get more pressing if ignored.

A UN report last month found the world was already on course to break through the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warming limit that countries had agreed to pursue under the 2015 Paris Agreement to prevent the worst effects of climate change.
“The situation could not be less under control. The planet is not dying. It is being killed,” Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg said on the sidelines of the UN conference.
“It is being killed by the very same people often thought to come to our rescue. No one is coming to our rescue.”
Earlier on Thursday, the leaders of small island states including the Bahamas, Tuvalu, the Solomon Islands and Saint Lucia called for swift action.
“Major emitters must move beyond the usual promises. They must reduce emissions that the climate crisis demands,” said Saint Lucia’s Prime Minister Philip J. Pierre.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham backed a proposal by Turkey to increase electricity’s share of world energy consumption to 35% by 2035, from a little over a fifth now, to help advance that goal. Turkey has not specified whether the extra energy used would be renewable.
Burnham told the conference that energy supply disruptions from the US-Israeli war with Iran and Russia’s war with Ukraine showed clean energy was the wise choice.

“It is now plain for everyone to see that if we depend on energy we do not control, then we leave ourselves exposed to prices we cannot control,” he said. “The shift to clean energy is the only route to energy security.”

Developing countries reiterated requests that they have made during many years of UN talks for rich countries to provide more finance to help them shift to cleaner energy, adapt to a warming world, and repair climate-driven destruction.

Fernanda de Carvalho, the head of climate policy for the World Wildlife Fund environmental group, said he found the leaders’ speeches underwhelming, especially as COP31 is the first UN conference since scientists have publicly said the world is set to breach the 1.5C threshold.
“It is worrying that the climate issue is not as high on the global political agenda as it needs to be,” he said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: U.S. envoys Kushner, Witkoff meet with Putin at Kremlin in talks to end Russia-Ukraine war
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys met with President Vladimir Putin on Thursday as Washington sought new momentum in peace efforts after two days of U.S.-mediated negotiations between Russian and…

image.caption: Russian President Vladimir Putin and Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov, left, are shown speaking to U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff on Thursday. Witkoff and fellow American envoy Jared Kushner were set to talk later in the day with Ukraine's president. (Vyacheslav Prokofiev/Sputnik/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys met with President Vladimir Putin on Thursday as Washington sought new momentum in peace efforts after two days of U.S.-mediated negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations.
U.S. envoys fly from Russia to Ireland to brief Zelenskyy after speaking to Putin

U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys met on Thursday with President Vladimir Putin as Washington sought new momentum in peace efforts after two days of U.S.-mediated negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations.

Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also Trump's son-in-law, brokered the talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, the first direct discussions between representatives of Moscow and Kyiv in nine months as the push for peace stalled.
The two days of talks that ended on Wednesday produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners, with the exact figure still to be announced.

Kushner and Witkoff met with Putin at the Kremlin and are scheduled to fly later to Dublin, Ireland, for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as Moscow's full-scale invasion nears the five-year mark.

Kushner said that one of the goals of the meeting with Putin was to get the Russian leader's blessing for European representatives to be part of the talks, which are looking at the continent's broader security arrangements.
The U.S. and Zelenskyy want Europe to appoint a single person to negotiate with Moscow.

But Moscow doesn't want European countries involved in the direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine's war effort. The Europeans are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent, and whether the U.S. will be too accommodating to Kremlin demands.
LISTEN | Reuters correspondent Dan Peleschuk on Ukrainian conscription controversies:
Front Burner21:55Ukrainian conscription in the crosshairs
Putin again warns against European troops

Many in Europe see the inclusion of Moscow in discussions about postwar European security as an unwelcome concession to Putin, who has described NATO's eastward expansion as a main security threat to Russia. Putin has demanded the transatlantic alliance's troops be pulled back from Russia's borders.
Some analysts say negotiators may be looking to grant Russia concessions on NATO's strategy in return for peace in Ukraine — a possibility that alarms European leaders.

items: Russia-Ukraine talks mediated by U.S. end with news of 'good momentum,' large-scale prisoner swap

blocks.text: Putin reaffirmed to the U.S. envoys Moscow's rejection of any European troop presence in Ukraine in a post-war scenario, saying that Russia sees them as a threat to its security and warns that they would be legitimate targets.
He also said Russia sees its border with Ukraine as the line of control — a reference to Moscow's claim over the four Ukrainian regions that Moscow annexed in 2022 but never fully captured.
Zelenskyy is in Dublin for a meeting of more than 40 European countries that also includes NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney was also present.
Rutte said the U.S., Europe and Ukraine are "very much aligned" on what security guarantees should look like, following a meeting in Paris in January.
"But now of course we need the peace deal, or at least a ceasefire," Rutte said.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stands next to French President Emmanuel Macron, centre, and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney as they pose for a photo along with other leaders at the European Political Community (EPC) Summit in Dublin, Ireland, on Thursday. (Peter Morrison/The Associated Press)
Zelenskyy called the proposed prisoner exchange a positive step but also insisted Ukraine won't surrender Russian-occupied territory in return for peace.
Russia and Ukraine have occasionally swapped prisoners, but both sides remain far apart in their terms for accepting a settlement.
Amid the negotiations, fighting continues along the 1,200-kilometre front line.

items: Putin pushes the myth of Russian invincibility, seemingly to set his terms for peace

blocks.text: Russia's bigger army has been held back by dogged Ukrainian resistance while Moscow's drone and missile strikes aim to deny civilians heat, electricity and running water, sapping public morale in what Kyiv calls a "weaponization of winter."
Zelenskyy says Starshield service disrupted again

Ukraine is experiencing another slowdown in the U.S. Starshield system — SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service — that the country needs to defend itself against Russian attacks, Zelenskyy said Thursday on social media.

Military units have recorded "significant disruptions," including speed restrictions limiting its drones to 161 kph, Zelenskyy said. He added that a military investigation established that the restrictions weren't random errors.
Ukraine uses Starlink and Starshield for intercepting Russian drones and launching its own mid- and long-range strikes.
Last month, limits on Ukrainian drone speeds severely disrupted operations and alarmed Kyiv officials who fear U.S. support could drop off.
Firefighters work on Thursday at an apartment building in Kyiv that was damaged following a Russian drone strike. (Gleb Garanich/Reuters)
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk acknowledged that his company had throttled the Starlink internet service in Ukraine for about a week, saying the system couldn't be used for offensive strikes against Russia.
Zelenskyy said in Dublin that the speed limits cover operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine and that Kyiv is trying to find out from U.S. officials what is going on.
"If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going," he said.

Russia's Defence Ministry said its air defences downed 71 Ukrainian drones overnight. Its forces struck a drone-making plant in Kyiv and three other facilities producing missile fuel and drone components in the area around the Ukrainian capital, the ministry said.
Russia launched missiles and 123 drones, 73 of them jet-powered drones, at Ukraine overnight, the Ukrainian air force said. Hits were recorded at 17 locations, it said.

articles.title: Brooklyn building collapse kills at least eight and injures 17 as search continues
articles.summary:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani says crews are working through ‘extremely dangerous conditions’ to find anyone trapped

Rescue crews have continued to search for survivors in the rubble of a collapsed…

blocks.text: Rescue crews have continued to search for survivors in the rubble of a collapsed building in Brooklyn, New York, as the death toll rose to eight.

Authorities in New York City said at least 17 people were hurt when the three-storey residential building on the edge of a construction site in the borough’s Flatbush neighbourhood collapsed at about 4pm on Wednesday.
Four people were critically injured, officials said, and at least seven children were among the casualties. It is not clear if any of the fatalities are minors.

Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City, said in a post on X on Thursday morning that he was “heartbroken” by the tragedy. “Eight New Yorkers have now lost their lives and at least 17 have been injured, including three firefighters,” he wrote.

blocks.caption: Zohran Mamdani said the conditions around the building were ‘extremely dangerous’ and urged people to stay away from the area. Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: “There are no words for a loss of this magnitude. My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we have lost, those who are injured and everyone grieving today.”

He urged the public to stay away from the site on Flatbush Avenue, where about 250 first responders from the New York City fire department (FDNY) worked through what Mamdani said were “extremely dangerous conditions” to find anybody still trapped.
The department, in an emailed statement to the New York Times on Thursday morning, said it was still hopeful of locating survivors.

Workers brought in an excavator in the early hours of Thursday to help move larger pieces of wreckage from the building, which had housed a number of apartments. Drones and canine units were being used to assist the rescue effort.

Video taken at the scene on Wednesday night showed crews removing several people on stretchers. One person, seen covered in dust, was extricated at about 6.30pm after a crew dug a hole through some of the debris.

blocks.caption: The building had housed a number of apartments.  Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: Another person rescued was a woman who was six months pregnant, whose husband had been searching for her through the late afternoon, New York ABC News affiliate WABC reported.
“I have an update. She is alive, she is still alive. I am very happy,” the man told the outlet.

Dozens of onlookers, some in tears, gathered to watch the rescue operation. Lillian Bonsignore, the FDNY commissioner, told a crowd at an evening press conference: “We know that we are not finished here, and we will likely not be finished for quite some time.”

Adding to the urgency of the situation was a weather forecast that predicted heavy rain with a chance of thunderstorms and gusty winds moving through the borough from lunchtime and through Thursday afternoon.

blocks.caption: Rescuers searching for people in the rubble a day after the Brooklyn building collapsed. Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: Several people who were made homeless by the collapse took shelter in the Bethesda church of God in Christ opposite the site.

The building that collapsed was perched at the edge of a lot where another one-storey building had been torn down for a construction project. The site was being excavated and the building that fell down filled the construction pit with bricks and wood.
Another building that shared a wall with the collapsed structure remained standing, but its wall was shorn off, exposing the rooms inside, including a bedroom and closets filled with clothing.
Investigators from New York City’s department of buildings were at the scene beginning an investigation into the cause of the collapse.

blocks.caption: A first responder on a crane illuminates the scene with a flashlight. Photograph: Ryan Murphy/AP

blocks.text: News channel NY1 reported that the department had recorded several issues with a project next door to the collapsed building in May, including working while there was a stop work order, not having proper overhead protection for the neighbouring properties, and failing to conform to approved construction drawings.
The city’s department of housing, preservation and development has recorded almost 100 violations at the collapsed building dating to 1972, NY1 said.
Property records show the building as a three-story construction containing four residential units and one commercial unit.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang steps down in big blow to AI boom
articles.summary: The departure could also have far-reaching consequences for US chip export policy, given Huang's push to preserve access to the Chinese market and his close ties with US President Donald Trump

blocks.text: BOSS. NVIDIA’s CEO Jensen Huang attends a media roundtable meeting in Singapore, on December 6, 2023.
Edgar Su/Reuters
The departure could also have far-reaching consequences for US chip export policy, given Huang's push to preserve access to the Chinese market and his close ties with US President Donald Trump

items: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is stepping down amid controversy over alleged affairs and potential espionage connections, leaving the company in uncertainty.
Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while Nvidia searches for a permanent replacement, and the company has appointed Harvey Jones as its first board chairman.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is stepping down, leaving the AI industry without its biggest champion and clouding the future of the chipmaker he built into an AI powerhouse.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO as Nvidia looks for a permanent successor, the company said on Thursday, November 12. It named former Synopsys CEO and board member Harvey Jones as its first-ever board chairman.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and is its fourth-largest investor with a stake of about 3.61%, will exit the board as well.
Nvidia shares fell more than 10% in premarket trading, and weighed on the broader market.
Pressure had been mounting on Huang in recent days after reports said the 63-year-old, who is married, had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing.

Nvidia’s board met on Wednesday, November 11, to consider his ouster, a person familiar with the matter said, after reports earlier in the day that Huang also had an extramarital affair with a senior company executive who reported to him.

Huang’s exit plunges the $4 trillion company into uncertainty and threatens to disrupt an AI ecosystem that he helped bankroll by pouring Nvidia’s swelling cash pile back into cloud providers, suppliers and the industry’s biggest labs.

“The risk is not that Nvidia suddenly loses its technology roadmap…that roadmap is largely visible for the next several years. The risk is execution. Jensen has been the chief conductor of an extraordinarily complex system,” said Michael Feldman, portfolio manager at ClearBridge Investments.
“In a world with real bottlenecks, that coordination is a competitive advantage in itself.”
Investor sentiment toward AI stocks has already been shaky as soaring cash burn and rising debt at traditionally cash-rich tech giants fuel doubts over whether the AI boom will pay off.
The departure could also have far-reaching consequences for US chip export policy, given Huang’s push to preserve access to the Chinese market and his close ties with US President Donald Trump.
Trump said on Sunday, November 8, that Huang had “done an amazing job for our country” and that the Nvidia chief had told him he had no idea the Chinese woman he had an affair with was a spy.

For years, Nvidia was best known to gamers chasing top-tier graphics. But its chips’ ability to perform many calculations at once has made them the oil of the AI boom and a strategic prize in the US-China race to dominate the technology. It also made Nvidia the world’s most valuable company.

That turned Huang into a rock-star CEO, mobbed by fans in Taiwan and South Korea who ask him to sign books, posters and sometimes even their bodies. Such is his pull that stocks moved at his mere mention of company names at events.

But scrutiny of his conduct has intensified in recent days after reports of his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed, who US authorities have concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.
The two, who have been photographed together in Taiwan, Singapore and California, are not related.

Washington has also investigated Megaspeed, a coveted official Nvidia cloud partner with priority access to its chips, over suspicions it helped China obtain advanced AI chips restricted under US export controls, according to media reports. Beijing has denied Alice Huang is a spy.

Earlier this month, Nvidia’s board launched a probe, led by independent directors with outside legal counsel, into whether Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. It also expressed confidence in him at the time.
The controversy escalated on Wednesday when the New York Times reported Huang also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reported to him. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Farage was guest on Brand podcast after sexual assault investigation began
articles.summary: Reform leader this week criticised the Labour party for ‘cosying up to’ and ‘promoting’ disgraced comedian

blocks.text: Nigel Farage appeared on Russell Brand’s US podcast nine months after the comedian was investigated by police over allegations of sexual assault, the Guardian has learned.

The Reform UK leader has criticised Labour for “cosying up to” and “promoting” Brand a decade ago, after the comedian was sentenced this week to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault.
It has now emerged that Farage was a guest on Brand’s online show in July 2024 – months after the sexual assault allegations were made public, but before he was charged in April 2025.

During the episode, Farage laughed with Brand about their shared interests in taking on the establishment and suggested the west had provoked Vladimir Putin into the Ukraine war because “what you don’t do with a Russian bear is deliberately poke it with a stick”.
Farage was aware of the serious sexual assault allegations against Brand at the time because he had commented on them on GB News the previous year, but they were not mentioned in the episode.

Sitting on a sofa together, alongside Dan Bongino, a Donald Trump supporter, and Charlie Kirk, the rightwing activist later murdered, Farage spoke of how “the old left-right divides” were being blown out of the water. He claimed that cancel culture meant people saying racist or homophobic things were “cancelled” but contempt for the white working class was allowed.
At the end of the show, Brand said: “Nigel, thank you for this impromptu opportunity to speak and I hope we get more chances to speak.”

A number of women accused Brand of sexual assault in a joint Sunday Times, Times and Channel 4 exposé in September 2023, and the comedian was subsequently interviewed under caution by police that autumn.

On GB News in September 2023, Farage said he was not a big fan of Brand but would not prejudge him and remarked on the comedian having “upset big government” and powerful men such as Bill Gates, an apparent reference to Brand’s anti-vaccine views.
On the allegations against the host, Farage said there was “no evidence being produced” and then referred to four or five women having come forward.

He added: “I’m not here to prejudge his guilt or his innocence, but there are many other things in his own autobiography that he’s written about his behaviour with women that are disturbing, abusive and not very pretty.”

Asked about his appearance with Brand, a spokesperson for Farage said: “Nigel regrets his appearance on the show. His thoughts are with the victims who have suffered immensely because of what Russell Brand has done.”
Reform sources said it was not a planned appearance, and he was pulled into the room during a visit to the US.
after newsletter promotion

Since the verdict, Farage has commented on the allegations against Brand on Australia’s News 24, saying: “It’s very difficult isn’t it, because this is two decades old, it’s ‘he said, she said’, although there’s more than one she. So these cases are always very difficult for us to judge at a distance because there is no actual hard evidence.”

blocks.caption: Russell Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault. Photograph: Brook Mitchell/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: However, he came out in support of Jemima Goldsmith, a former partner of Brand, who has accused him of assault. Farage said she was known to him and he believed her account of Brand being violent and abusive, adding: “The judicial system has proved to have actually worked.”
He also criticised Labour for failing to apologise for “cosying up” to Brand a decade ago.

It is not the first time Farage has met a man accused of abusive behaviour. The Reform UK leader was pictured with Andrew Tate, the misogynist influencer, in 2019. Tate was charged with rape and human trafficking in 2023, and the UK is now seeking to extradite him from the US. Tate denies the allegations.

Farage spoke in favour of Tate for defending “male culture” in a Strike It Big podcast which aired in February 2024, while acknowledging that the influencer had gone “over the top” and that he had said some “pretty horrible” things.

Asked about his podcast appearance and comments on Tate, Farage said: “There’s an awakening in a younger generation who have had enough of being dictated to, have had enough of being lectured to. They’re seeing through the rubbish they’re getting taught in schools and universities. If no other politician is willing to reach out to this group of people, then I will.”

articles.title: Iran: Exiled journalists still repressed by regime
articles.summary: For many independent reporters, leaving Iran does not mean fully escaping the grasp of the Iranian state. The regime uses family members, bank accounts and the property they left behind to apply…
articles.byline: Shabnam von Hein, Khoshhal Soustani Pouyan

image.caption: Journalists outside Iran say their families face pressure and threatsImage: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: In times of crisis, Iran's political system is looking for scapegoats — and independent journalists, even journalists who have been living in exile for a long time, are high on their list.

At the end of September, Iran's judiciary announced that it had confiscated assets belonging to individuals accused of "cooperation with hostile governments." The measure is part of a previously announced plan targeting around 400 people living abroad, including journalists, activists, artists and athletes, whose assets are to be seized.

"The only thing I own in my parents' house in Iran is a bookshelf," says Amir Soltanzadeh. The exiled freelance journalist, who occasionally works for Germany's international broadcaster DW, discovered his name on a government list, which Iranian state media had labeled "traitors to the homeland." His assets were to be seized. In an online post earlier this year, he published a photo of his book collection and wrote: "This library is my only asset in Iran. If you enjoy reading books, go ahead and confiscate them."
'My father lost his job because of me'

Soltanzadeh said that his bank account in Iran was also frozen. It contained the equivalent of around €500 ($555), which he used, among other things, to buy his family members gifts and flowers for special occasions. He noted it was "unjust" to list him as a traitor.
"I have not acted against Iran," he stressed. "Every position I have taken was ultimately aimed at improving the lives of people in Iran."
Iran's regime: inside the system protecting its rulers
Some of his relatives, he said, have cut ties with his family because of his journalistic work.

"When people hear about a journalist working abroad, some who adopt the government's narrative automatically equate that person with a spy. They see a journalist as someone who is paid to gather information," said Soltanzadeh.
This pressure, according to the exiled journalist, eventually extended to his father's workplace.
"My father lost his job because of me. And because of me, my mother lives in constant anxiety — every time the phone rings, she has to wonder who is on the other end."
For several months, Soltanzadeh also cut all direct contact with his family to keep them safe, and only communicated with them through an intermediary.
Regime using vague laws to control media reporting

Pressure against independent journalists is a part of a recurring pattern in the Islamic Republic. In times of political tension, Western media outlets and journalists are often portrayed as agents of hostile intelligence services such as the CIA or Mossad, or mouthpieces spreading subversive propaganda.
The authorities have many tools to spy on reporters, including hacking their social media accounts and intercepting conversations that are later used as evidence against their contacts inside Iran.
Such forms of repression also affect which information ends up reaching the public.
Young Iranians use dance to protest
A journalist in Iran, who wanted to stay anonymous, says that reporting on detainees, state executions and the treatment of protesters comes with major risks and restrictions.
"Journalists can only write on their personal pages in a very limited and censored way," the reporter said. "In their reports, they are required to follow the government's official narrative."

Iran-based journalists have to weigh potential legal consequences of their work. This, in turn, constrains their ability to conduct independent research, maintain contact with sources and pursue sensitive topics.

Article 24 of Iran's constitution guarantees freedom of the press. However, the Press Law has been amended and expanded several times over the past four decades. It requires media professionals, among other things, not to endanger the Islamic Republic, not to insult the clergy or the Supreme Leader, and not to disseminate false information. These broadly worded provisions give authorities significant room to interfere in the work of the media.
Danger follows reporters abroad
Many journalists are forced to leave the country due to the constant pressure and the risk of being targeted by the authorities.
"Because of my journalistic work, I had to go into exile," says Omid Barin, a freelance journalist who also occasionally contributes to DW.

Barin's reporting focuses on issues such as human rights violations and the position of ethnic minorities in Iran. The pressure "has undoubtedly caused me to be much more cautious and sensitive when communicating with sources inside the country, to avoid putting them in danger," he told DW.

While Barin chooses not to provide details on the threats he faces, citing the risk of backlash on the people close to him, he says the core message behind them is clear: Someone in Iran would like him to either abandon journalism or steer away from sensitive topics.

Even while living abroad, Barin is forced to take additional precautions in his daily life and pay close attention to his personal security due to his work for media outlets that the Iranian regime considers "hostile."
Unbreakable: My fight for freedom in Iran

Just 28.2% of 18- and 19-year-olds have received their first dose in one-off campaign, UKHSA says

The clock is ticking for young people in the UK to receive vaccinations to protect against…

blocks.text: The clock is ticking for young people in the UK to receive vaccinations to protect against meningitis B, experts have said, as figures reveal fewer than one in three eligible in one-off campaign have received their first dose.

Earlier this year an unprecedented outbreak of meningitis B in Kent and clusters of cases in Dorset and Berkshire caused three deaths, as well as life-long health consequences among some of those who survived.
As a result, the government announced in June a one-off, time-limited programme offering young adults two doses of a vaccine that protects against most strains of MenB bacteria.

But figures from the UK Health Security Agency have revealed just 28.2% of 18- and 19-year-olds have received a first dose. Dr Shamez Ladhani, consultant epidemiologist at the UKHSA, said time was running out for young people to get both doses of the vaccine, and urged those eligible to book an appointment.
He said: “The deadline for getting your first dose is 31 December, so please don’t leave it until the end of term or forget it amongst all the Christmas and other holiday festivities.”

Prof Andrew Pollard, director of the Oxford Vaccine Group, also raised concerns. He said: “While we can’t be sure whether there will be more student outbreaks of meningitis, as happened earlier this year in Kent, it is very worrying to me that uptake is so low.
“MenB vaccines can’t stop all cases, but they are still highly effective. It would be a tragedy if even one preventable case were to occur, when we have the tools to keep our young people safe.”

Two doses of the vaccine, given at least 28 days apart, are needed for protection, with UKHSA noting a second dose will be available until 31 March 2027. The latest data suggests almost 70% of 18- and 19-years-olds who have received a first dose have already had their second dose.

According to UKHSA, all those born between 1 September 2007 and 31 August 2008, are eligible for the vaccinations, as well as people under the age of 25 who started university, or residential further education, for the first time this autumn.

UKHSA said freshers had a risk about seven times higher than their peers who did not go to university. Experts have said factors such as shared accommodation, parties and large social networks can aid the spread of the bacteria.

Dr Eliza Gil, a clinical lecturer at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, said the peak season for invasive MenB infection was typically December to March. She said: “The decision to make the vaccine offer time limited likely reflects both modelled cost effectiveness and an attempt to ensure eligible young people have their first vaccine dose before peak season, so that they have immune protection by the time they are most likely to be exposed.

“Although the overall risk of MenB remains low, if eligible young people are not vaccinated in sufficient numbers, or in time for peak season, the vaccine programme is likely to be less effective in preventing further outbreaks.”
after newsletter promotion

Henry Gregg, chief executive of the National Pharmacy Association, said further action was needed to promote the offer. He said: “This should also include universities promoting this campaign strongly to those living in residential accommodation.”

Dr Michael Head, associate professor in global public health at the University of Southampton, said there was a case for reconsidering the December deadline, alongside enhanced health promotion campaigns.

“The risk of meningitis doesn’t suddenly disappear on 1 January. Young people will continue to mix inside and outside of universities,” he said. “I would also favour a wider review of whether MenB vaccination should routinely be offered to adolescents.”

The charity Meningitis Now and the National Union of Students also back routine MenB vaccination for young people; while earlier this year the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation recommended a routine single MenB booster jab for 15-year olds who had menB vaccinations as infants, with two doses for those who missed out.

Gregg said an annual campaign should replace an ad-hoc, standalone event. He said: “MenB is an extremely serious illness and we must do all we can to minimise the risk of tragic outbreaks that we have already seen this year in Kent, Berkshire and Dorset.”
