articles.title: DOJ open to exemptions to abortion as a crime amid drafting of criminal code
articles.summary: Justice Undersecretary Raul Vasquez said the Department of Justice (DOJ) maintains that abortion is a crime but added that the DOJ was open to proposing exemptions with proposed amendments to the…

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 10:08pm

Justice Undersecretary Raul Vasquez said the Department of Justice (DOJ) maintains that abortion is a crime but added that the DOJ was open to proposing exemptions with proposed amendments to the Revised Penal Code (RPC) pending before the House of Representatives.
At a news briefing, Vasquez said that a DOJ committee has prepared a draft Criminal Code of the Philippines which aims to amend the RPC.
Asked about several laws that could change with the code, Vasquez said there has been an effort by some progressive lawmakers to decriminalize abortion.
“Our position in the DOJ is that abortion is okay as a crime still because of the constitutional mandate. At the same time, our culture still prohibits such conduct,” Vasquez said.

“We are also open to the possibility of giving exemptions like for therapeutic purposes or… I have even instructed our prosecutors or committee members who are attending there actively under my guidance, I have asked them also to be open to the possibility of allowing that in, for instance, rape,” he added.
Other matters being discussed was the topic of adultery and concubinage.

Under Philippine law, adultery is committed by a married woman who had sexual intercourse with a man, while concubinage is when a married man keeps a mistress under certain circumstances, including having intercourse with her and cohabiting a place with her.

“That is one of the major reforms we initiated because there really is a huge divide between adultery and concubinage. So the proposal is to make it equal… I would say that it is quite controversial, even in the discussion before the House of Representatives, because there is a resistance to do it in the same way,” Vasquez said.

“Adultery is committed by a single act of sexual misconduct committed by a married woman, on the other hand, concubinage requires certain circumstances or factors to be considered before they could be prosecuted,” he added.
Other laws being considered for revision included laws on espionage and libel, according to the DOJ executive. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: NAZA: how and where to watch the Guardian’s acclaimed Gaza documentary
articles.summary:
Film features testimony from 24 Israeli officials involved in surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians

• NAZA is in cinemas worldwide and will screen for free on the…

blocks.text: Where can I watch the film?
NAZA will be released in full on the Guardian’s website for free in early December. Sign up here to be notified of the exact streaming date and to be sent a link to the film when it is live.

NAZA has been shown by cinemas in 47 countries and seen by more than 1.5 million people since its release last month, making it one of the most-watched documentary films with a theatrical release in 2026. The film has been offered to a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel but has not been screened there yet.
You can watch a trailer here.

blocks.caption: Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the directors of NAZA, take questions after its UK premiere at the Ritzy cinema in south London. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: What is NAZA about?

NAZA is a documentary featuring testimony from 24 Israeli military intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians during the war in Gaza. The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to civilians expected to be killed in a military attack.

The interviewees detail the methods used by the Israeli military in Gaza, including AI-based systems built to identify large numbers of potential Hamas operatives, who were then bombed in their homes at night, in the knowledge that the attacks would also kill their families.

Interviews were filmed at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv, on the condition of anonymity, because of the risks involved in speaking publicly. The appearance and voices of participants in the film have been digitally altered to disguise their identities.
Who is behind the film?

The film was directed by the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian. It builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian magazine +972, the Hebrew-language news outlet Local Call and the Guardian newspaper between 2023 and 2025.

Abraham and Szor were two of the four co-directors – with the Palestinians Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal – of No Other Land, which documents the destruction of Masafer Yatta, a village in the occupied West Bank targeted by Israeli forces. It won the Oscar for best documentary in 2025.
NAZA was co-produced by James Wilson and executive-produced by Jonathan Glazer, the team behind the Oscar-winning film The Zone of Interest.

blocks.caption: NAZA features interviews with Israeli officials who explain the targeting of presumed Hamas operatives. Photograph: NAZA/The Guardian

blocks.text: How has it been received?

NAZA has received widespread critical acclaim and is selling out in cinemas across the world. The New York Times says it is “tough to watch and impossible to ignore”, while New York Magazine describes it as “one of the most important films of our time”. In a five-star review, the Financial Times says that “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film”.

The film won the special jury prize at the Venice film festival in September, where its premiere had a 25-minute ovation – a festival record. In November, it won the best political documentary from the Critics Choice Association.
Why has there been an Israeli backlash?

The film, its directors and their confidential sources have faced fierce attacks from the Israeli government and military. The prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of sources interviewed and prosecute them for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

Netanyahu also threatened to strip Abraham and Szor of their citizenship, accusing them of treason. The Israeli military’s chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, said the military would “not allow soldiers to be made targets through lies and blood libels” and would use “every tool at our disposal” against the film.

Far-right groups have vowed to hound the film-makers on their return to Israel and picketed Szor’s family home. Some of the messages included explicit calls for violence, with one protester demanding the “death penalty for traitors”.

The Israeli military claimed there were “substantial errors” in the film and that it had relied on sources who had only a partial picture of the target approval process. It said that while AI was used to help identify targets in Gaza, final decisions on strikes, and the risk of civilian casualties, were signed off by officers.
In response, the team behind the film have revealed they spoke to more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.
What is NAZA: The Real Story?

The Israeli government is promoting an online film project, called NAZA: The Real Story, which mimics the style of the genuine NAZA film and is hosted on a website called nazadocumentary.com. It is not the real NAZA documentary and has been misleading some viewers.

Initially, the rival film’s website falsely presented itself as a promotional page for NAZA itself, naming Abraham and Szor as the directors, and listing film festivals where the documentary was to be screened. The site now appears as a platform for the rival film, which has been promoted by Israeli embassies.

Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who co-created NAZA: The Real Story, describes it as an “offensive move” to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians.
Szor and Abraham have addressed the backlash to their documentary. “Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor said.

articles.title: Two men found guilty over Iranian attempts to ‘eliminate’ UK-based journalists
articles.summary:
Mostafa Sepahvand and Farhad Javadi Manesh carried out surveillance in an effort to inflict violence on three people

Two men of Iranian origin who were hired through social media as part of…

blocks.text: Two men of Iranian origin who were hired through social media as part of a plan to “eliminate” journalists in the UK have been found guilty of engaging in conduct likely to assist Tehran’s intelligence services.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, carried out surveillance and reconnaissance between August 2024 and March last year in an attempt to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK.

These subjects included two journalists for the London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, and a founder member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner.

The defendants visited addresses linked to their targets, took photos and videos and used platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online. They appear to be part of a growing new tactic used by hostile states in which “proxies” are hired to work for foreign security forces, with often little idea who they are targeting or why.

Last month the Norwegian teenager Johannes Natland, 19, was jailed for life after he agreed to carry out a hit in Huddersfield for the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.
The Iranian men came to the UK illegally between 2016 and 2022 – Sepahvand in the back of a lorry and Manesh in a small boat.

Sepahvand used the AI platform ChatGPT to find the home address of Mojtaba Pourmohsen who worked for London-based Persian language broadcaster Iran International. He hoped to earn £150,000 to carry out a violent attack and help to “finish off” Pourmohsen.
Sepahvand chatted on WhatsApp to his handler, an IRGC commander called Amin, as he spied on Pourmohsen in December 2024, Woolwich crown court heard.
Amin wrote: “These are new pictures of the guy/bloke.”
Sepahvand replied: “I’ll go tomorrow.”
Referring to a picture, Amin said: “And that dot is their office?”
Sepahvand said: “Love you brother, I’ll go there tomorrow.”
The pair also discussed surveillance of Iranian satirist Kambiz Hosseini, who eventually had to leave home because of the threats made against him.

Bill Emlyn Jones KC, prosecuting, said the Islamic Republic of Iran and its rulers do not and cannot tolerate dissent. “One organisation critical to the regime, and therefore very much in its sights, is Iran International, a news organisation which has come under particular attack because of its explicit support for opposition groups and its editorial stance, which is anti-Islamic Republic of Iran.
“Eliminating hostile, critical or dissident actors overseas is a staple policy of the Islamic Republic. Together, the defendants were engaged in what is very obviously a form of spying,” Jones said.

Hosseini, 51, had to leave home and stop work as a standup comedian as a result of the threats he received. He was sent a message with a picture of his car saying the next time he started the engine it would blow up. Hosseini’s family in Iran also received threats, and his family had to leave the country.
The court heard Sepahvand had been convicted of theft in Iran and was drawn into the plan to “eliminate” dissidents in the hope of reducing his criminal record.
after newsletter promotion
He told his Iranian handlers he was prepared to escalate from surveillance to violence, the court heard.

He hoped to receive a final payment of £150,000 for “finishing the job”, a reference to killing one of the journalists, the court was told. “If the person [the target] is inside, they pay the £150,000, and I’ll finish him off,” said Sepahvand in a voice note.
Sepahvand claimed his family were being threatened and he never intended to go through with the hit. He also denied plotting to kill Jonathan Turner of UK Lawyers for Israel.
Manesh claimed he took a picture of the Iran International site because it was “a beautiful building” and did not know they were working with the Iranian intelligence services.

Earlier this year, Roman Lavrynovych, 22, and Stanislav Carpiuc, 27, were jailed at the Old Bailey for seven and two years respectively for arson attacks on property connected to Keir Starmer. An anonymous Russian-speaking figure named El Money had recruited Lavrynovych and Carpiuc on Telegram.

Last year, six Britons were jailed for their parts in a Russian-ordered arson attack on a London warehouse providing aid to Ukraine. The ringleader, Dylan Earl, was recruited by the Wagner group, a mercenary organisation that acts on behalf of the Russian state.

Sepahvand was convicted by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct. Manesh was convicted of assisting a foreign intelligence service, but cleared of preparatory conduct.
Shapoor Noori, 57, of Ealing, was cleared by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct.
Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb remanded Sepahvand and Manesh ahead of sentencing at the Old Bailey on 17 December.

articles.title: What’s behind Australia’s surge in teen extremism?
articles.summary:
Young people are being found with ‘hard drives full of what can only be described as gore’, one expert says

In March, Guardian Australia revealed that most people

blocks.text: In March, Guardian Australia revealed that most people who have been charged with the new federal crime of possession of violent extremist material are under 18.
This week Australian federal police sounded the alarm about a surge in teen extremism: 32 of the 37 young people prosecuted in counter-terrorism cases since 2020 were charged in the past two years.

The growth in youth extremism is happening within a sprawling online ecosystem. My investigations have tracked the rise of online networks that urge violence and nihilism for their own sake, in which perpetrators coerce victims not much younger than themselves to commit brutal and degrading acts.

In a review of 55 youth terrorism cases, the AFP has found that the profile is mixed. They are often young men. Many have received some support or intervention for a mental health condition. Some are from stable homes, others not.
What they have most in common is that they are young people on the internet. Experts say the age of those caught up in these crimes is decreasing.
In the last month two teenagers in Darwin have been charged with collecting documents that could facilitate acts of terrorism.

The second teenager was arrested after an initial examination of documents and electronic devices at a Northern Territory home, according to the AFP, allegedly found material and online discussions “including glorification of mass casualty attacks at schools”.

The arrests came five months after another NT teenager was charged with making posts with “pro-Nazi, anti-immigration, anti-trans and white nationalist themes”. The charge sheet alleges he also possessed videos of white nationalist terrorist attacks, including the 2019 Christchurch mosque shooting and the 2022 Buffalo shooting that it partly inspired.
All matters are still before the courts.
Experts involved in harm prevention programs, including the Victoria University professor Debra Smith, have watched the age of this cohort decrease dramatically over the past decade.

Instead of considering the challenge exclusively through the lens of radicalisation, Smith says we need to recognise that some young people are being socialised and finding identity in online spaces that may appear exciting and transgressive but are ultimately harmful to themselves, and may encourage them to do harm to others.
She has seen cases where teenagers are being found with “hard drives full of what can only be described as gore”.

“It’s like getting involved in any other … unhealthy subcultural aspect of life … [such as] gangs or crime for payment,” she says. “There’s this offering of what young people can look at and get involved in that just simply wasn’t there years ago.”

The Guardian’s investigation into the growth of extremist material charges, as well as the surge of young people in Australia ensnared in sadistic online extortion and gore networks, reveals an amorphous online ecosystem in which young people may easily come into contact with extreme and violent content.

A teenager in New South Wales who pleaded guilty to possessing violent extremist material, among other charges, described how he first came across such content on TikTok when he was 14 and sought validation by talking to others online. He used ChatGPT to research the Boston marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev as well as security arrangements at the Sydney Opera House. He was sentenced to a three-year community corrections order.
Others have told police how they became involved in so-called “gore” channels on Telegram, where more and more extreme footage – including of animal abuse –is traded.
after newsletter promotion

Given the age of many involved, Levi West, a research fellow at the Australian National University, says they may be considered as much victims as perpetrators, which is a significant challenge for how authorities respond.

It’s important for parents, schools and others to think about what’s sitting underneath the uptick in numbers, he says, and not just the “algorithms”. He points to the legacies of Covid-19 and lockdowns as well as the presence of screens and digital technologies in the lives of young people.
“We are not going to arrest our way out of this problem,” West says.
With people as young as 13 before the courts, Australia must consider if authorities are taking the right approach and have the right resources for this challenge.

The Guardian’s investigation into the possession of extremist material charges in South Australia and around the country found that many of those who had been before the courts faced a range of health and social difficulties, including autism diagnoses and learning challenges – and raised questions about whether some young people understand a crime has been committed.
Smith has seen many young people caught up in these activities who come from troubled family backgrounds, while others have had every opportunity in life.

There is a role for everyone involved in caring for young people, she says, from parents and schools to sporting clubs, to recognise when someone might be engaging in harmful behaviours long before there is a risk of violence, then help them access non-punitive pathways for help.
“It’s really important to understand it through a developmental lens – that these are young people who are making decisions with young brains,” Smith says.
“My grave concern is that if we are just giving everyone terrorism offences at [age] 12, 13, 14, 15, we’re starting to label them the thing that they will become.”

articles.title: Icac’s drama and dirt files show NSW’s ‘guns for hire’ problem. But neither major party is serious about reform
articles.summary:
Chris Minns is trying to address the threat of undeclared lobbying but falls well short of what the commission recommended five years ago

  • Get our

blocks.text: A dirt file on a state minister peddled to journalists. A subterranean campaign to discredit the building commissioner. Convincing the Liberal party to unseat councillors in the Hills district who were blocking a developer.

The New South Wales corruption watchdog’s recent inquiry, Rosny, revealed the ease with which the key protagonists – a group of rightwing Liberal operatives known as the Reformers, all of whom were former staffers – could move along the corridors of NSW parliament.

The Independent Commission against Corruption (Icac) has alleged that, unbeknown to their fellow Liberals, the operatives – including the then treasurer, Dominic Perrottet’s own brother Charles Perrottet – were being paid $2m by one of NSW’s most notorious developers, Jean Nassif, and that they worked to progress his interests.
Only one of the rightwing operatives involved in the Rosny inquiry was a registered lobbyist and subject to rules about declaring his clients and keeping records of interactions with ministers.

Yet all of them were on first name terms with many of their former colleagues and bureaucrats, affording them easy access for a chin-wag or to mix with powerful players – especially within the Liberal party’s machine.

Nassif – who told Icac he was “not corrupt” – has fled to Lebanon after the collapse of his company Toplace, leaving hundreds of buyers with substandard buildings. Charles Perrottet has repeatedly denied taking payments from Nassif for political outcomes. Dominic Perrottet is not a person of interest in Icac’s inquiry and is not accused of any wrongdoing.

The issue of access for former staffers – whether they be third-party lobbyists employed by specialist lobbying firms who are “guns for hire”, or “government relations” specialists employed directly by companies or industry groups – has long been a concern for Icac.
As Rosny showed, there was no way politicians could know who some of these figures were working for because these were allegedly undeclared guns for hire.

The NSW Labor government has now introduced a bill to clarify obligations for at least one class of lobbyist: the guns for hire. It passed the lower house on Wednesday, though it may not become law before the election.
Chris Minns’ efforts to address the threat that undeclared lobbying poses fall well short of what Icac recommended five years ago.
First, the good bits of the proposed legislation.

It would formally establish the NSW Electoral Commission as the regulator of third party lobbyists and bolster its investigative powers to audit compliance with the Lobbying of Government Officials Act and lobbyists code of conduct.
Icac recommended a separate lobbying commissioner but, given the electoral commission already has responsibility for the register, Minns has proposed it get the job.

“Third-party lobbyists are already subject to information and disclosure obligations, including disclosing information to the electoral commission for publication on the lobbyists register,” the special minister of state, John Graham, told Guardian Australia.

blocks.caption: Screengrab of individuals questioned in Operation Rosny, an Icac investigation. Left to right, top row: Jean Nassif, Jeremy Greenwood and Charles Perrottet. Bottom row: Damien Tudehope, Sharangan Maheswaran and Anita Perrottet.  Composite: ICAC

blocks.text: “The bill would allow the NSW Electoral Commission to audit compliance of third-party lobbyists and require relevant accounts, documents, information and explanations.”

It also extends the act to third party lobbyists interacting with councils. Lobbyists interacting with councils will need to register and adhere to the code. This had been identified by Icac as a gap that needed fixing.
But the bill also has bad bits. It ignores some of Icac’s most important recommendations.

The most glaring loophole is that the disclosure regime doesn’t extend to staff employed directly by companies – usually with a title like “government relations” or “corporate affairs” – even through they also lobby politicians.
These individuals make up about 80% of the people floating round the corridors of power. Most are former political staff members.

Graham said registering in-house lobbyists would have “created unnecessary red tape given it is already clear whose interests are being served or represented, and ministerial diary disclosures provide transparency of lobbyists’ interaction”.

This ignores the need for record keeping under the lobbyist regulations. If inhouse lobbyists were subject to the rules, they would be obliged to keep records of who they lobbied, as would the ministers and bureaucrats who were approached.
The government argues it plans to enhance ministerial diary disclosures, to make them fully searchable, rather than issuing them quarterly in pdf form.
The legislation will also clarify that third party lobbyists will need to disclose attendance at fundraising events involving exclusive or private access to a minister.
But the bill does not extend to lobbyists’ interactions with key ministerial staff, such as their chief of staff – which Operation Rosny demonstrated were important conduits to the minister.
“We’re regulating ministers and senior public servants because they’re decision makers. Ministerial staff are not decision makers,” Graham said.
Chiefs of staff can be almost as powerful as their minister, because they control access – and can direct policy staff.

Operation Rosny heard allegations about how the Liberal operatives, in their quest to smear the reputation of the building commissioner, provided material to a chief of staff, who then passed it to the chief of staff for the minister responsible for the building commissioner. The Liberal figures denied to Icac they were seeking to remove the building commissioner on behalf of Nassif.
Icac also heard evidence that Charles Perrottet talked to ministers directly about the building commissioner. He was not a registered lobbyist, yet he enjoyed extraordinary access and influence.
Neither the chiefs of staff nor the ministers were aware that Charles Perrottet was being paid by Nassif via a lobbying firm.

The government has also watered down Icac’s proposals for a six-month prohibition on certain public service roles taking on lobbying roles in either lobbying firms or private enterprise when leaving the bureaucracy.
Icac wanted certain sensitive roles to require six months’ “gardening leave” – as occurs when public servants leave the state’s gambling regulator.
If the bill ever reaches the upper house – and its future is now uncertain – debate is likely to be feisty.

The Greens have introduced a private member’s bill into parliament that would implement most of Icac’s recommendations from five years ago – including extending the lobbyists scheme to inhouse lobbyists.
Kobi Shetty, the minor party’s anti-corruption spokesperson, said her bill would have included a four-year exclusion for some public sector employees.
“When industries with deep pockets get a louder voice than the communities affected by their decisions, public trust in our democracy is eroded,” Shetty says.
The Centre for Public Integrity senior counsel Geoffrey Watson says the government’s bill is a step in the right direction and he hopes it passes the Legislative Council.
But he wishes the government had been more ambitious.

articles.title: NSW’s latest news Instagram account has an unlikely group behind it: the Labor party
articles.summary:
Expert warns of ‘huge loophole in political communication laws’ as state government among parties presenting accounts as unaffiliated news sources

  • Get our
articles.byline: Penry Buckley, Josh Butler and Bertin Huynh

blocks.text: “Breaking,” a reel from the Instagram account nswnewsroom reads. “Another Liberal MP quits, almost a third now gone.”

The post looks like it could have been made by a media outlet. It cites the source as the Daily Telegraph and Jordan Lane, a New South Wales MP, who is the sixth sitting Liberal member to announce they won’t re-contest their seat at the March 2027 election.
But the account’s bio tells a different story: it was authorised by the NSW Labor state secretary.

The account, which first posted two weeks ago and says “keep up to date with with [sic] news from NSW govt” in its bio, is part of an increasingly common tactic where Australian political parties set up accounts that appear at first glance to be unaffiliated news sources. The accounts feature different names and imagery without prominent party branding, to promote specific messages or highlight their own side.

Andrew Hughes, an expert in political marketing at the Australian National University, said these types of accounts take advantage of a “huge loophole in our political communication laws in Australia when it comes to digital and social media communications”.
“More and more of us get our news and information primarily from digital and social media,” said Hughes.

“There’s more and more potential for that information to be used against voters who aren’t engaged with politics or the news to a really good level of detail to spot disinformation and misinformation,” he said.

As unpaid content, the posts are not subject to the same authorisation requirements as paid advertisements at state and federal level. In NSW, an authorisation in the account profile or a website directly linked to that post is acceptable. The nswnewsroom account added its authorisation after reporting by the Sydney Morning Herald.

A spokesperson for the NSW government referred Guardian Australia to a statement shared with the paper, which said the page was “a Labor-affiliated social media page, consistent with the practices of most major political parties and a number of minor parties across Australia”.

In Victoria a similar account, vicnewstoday, was set up ahead of this month’s Victorian state election. While the account bio contains an authorisation by Victorian Labor HQ, the posts, including videos of Ben Carroll and ministers at press conferences, do not. In one, captioned “BREAKING: Liberals did a deal with ‘the most anti-worker party’”, Carroll criticises a preference deal between the Liberals and One Nation.
In late October, the Labor party launched a page titled “Don’t Risk It Vic”, promoting posts that raise concerns about an alliance between the Liberal and One Nation parties.
Meta’s ad library reveals that page was the highest-spending political advertiser in the country last week, paying $67,138 to promote its posts between 31 October and 6 November.
A spokesperson for the Victorian Labor Party said social media was “an important way to communicate with Victorians where they are, particularly those who don’t engage with traditional media”.
“There is a lot at stake for Victoria. And everyone deserves to hear the facts about what a Liberal-One Nation government would mean for our health system, schools, police and cost-of-living.”

Monica Attard, former Media Watch host, now professor of journalism practice at the University of Technology, Sydney, said in an age where social media was “awash with deepfakes”, it was “really important for consumers – and probably equally important for political parties – to disclose clearly and always”.
“I would think that the possibility of misuse or tampering would be relatively high.”
Ahead of the 2025 federal election, Guardian Australia uncovered a string of similar social media pages set up by Labor, the Coalition, Climate 200 and campaign group Advance.

All pages carried basic authorisation messages from their creators, but the page names and profile pictures did not immediately denote the source. Labor state divisions in NSW and Western Australia set up at least two anti-Peter Dutton pages, with posts raising doubts about health spending and WA’s GST deal under a Coalition government.

The Liberal party launched a page called “Teals Revealed”, scrutinising the voting record of Climate 200-backed independents, while Climate 200, in turn, set up “Independent News”, to promote news about crossbench MPs.

articles.title: House OKs bill allowing students with unpaid fees to join graduation rites
articles.summary: The House of Representatives has approved on second reading House Bill 11579 or the Kapakanan ng Magsisipagtapos Bill, which prohibits schools from denying a graduating student with financial or…

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 9:57pm

The House of Representatives has approved on second reading House Bill 11579 or the Kapakanan ng Magsisipagtapos Bill, which prohibits schools from denying a graduating student with financial or property obligations from participating in graduation ceremonies.

"The proposal is to allow students with outstanding property or money obligations, financial obligations to higher education institutions to be able to participate in the graduation ceremonies," House Committee on Higher Education chairperson Representative Jude Acidre said in an interview Thursday.

When asked what will happen to the students' financial or property obligations, Acidre replied, "It does not absolve them of the obligations. Hindi po quits sa mga eskwelahan ang mga kailangan bayaran."

"Pero at the very least, sana hayaan silang makapagmartsa sa entablado. ...Kasi sa tingin natin, maliit man bagay isipin, pero kasama po ng pagmartsa ng isang estudyante ang mga hinaing, ang mga pangarap, at ang tagumpay ng kanilang mga mahal sa buhay," Acidre added.

The Tingog Party-list representative also clarified that the bill also seeks to "protect also the rights of the school, and we want to make sure that this does not result in an unfair arrangement to them."
"So they are still empowered to hold the documents, the transcripts, the diploma, from being released to the students, pending the fulfillment of these financial and property obligations," he added.

The proposed measure empowers the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) and the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) to prescribe sanctions for schools that violate the measure. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Poundland owner secures two extra weeks to ensure retail chain’s survival
articles.summary: US investment firm Gordon Brothers is ‘taking due care’ to consider if one of three bidders has enough funds

blocks.text: Poundland’s owner has said it is “taking due care” to consider if one of three bidders had enough funds to ensure its survival after the troubled budget retail chain secured two more weeks to find a deal.

The management of Poundland, which employs approximately 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, won approval from the high court for an extension of legal protection from creditors on Thursday morning.
Poundland’s board said it had sought the extra time “with a view to identifying the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and our people”.
It added: “Our stores remain open as usual during this period and we thank our colleagues, suppliers and customers for their incredible and continued support.”

The retail chain’s owner, the US investment firm Gordon Brothers, has been under pressure to accept a bid for the company that would save retail jobs and protect thousands of suppliers since Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators two weeks ago.

A spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said on Thursday: “We support the board’s decision to extend the legal moratorium over the company by a further 10 working days. This brings additional stability amid an ongoing sale process in the backdrop of increasing cost pressures and a difficult inflationary economic environment.

“With this decision, we are today able to confirm to Poundland employees that funds will be released to allow payroll to be made in full this month, while additional funds continue to be released to support Poundland’s ongoing trading.
“We are in discussions with three parties for a sale of the whole business, and we have also received several offers from established high street retailers for significant parts of the business.

“While our preference remains a sale of the whole company, we are taking due care to ensure that any successful offer can provide the funds required to acquire the business and see it through to sustainable cash generation. We, the board, and all involved are working to secure a credible plan that delivers certainty, preserves value and protects as many jobs as possible.”
Gordon Brothers confirmed it had provided £85m of financing, understood to be via an asset-backed loan that Poundland has only partially used over the past year.
That financing is in addition to a £30m shareholder loan largely taken on by Gordon Brothers when it bought the business for a nominal £1 last year.
after newsletter promotion
Gordon Brothers fought back after MPs on Wednesday accused the Poundland owner of extracting millions of pounds from the retailer when it was on a “knife-edge”.
Documents provided to MPs showed the finance firm had taken close to £20m in interest payments and various fees, including those relating to store closures since acquiring Poundland.
Gordon Brothers said it had provided finance for Poundland “when no one else was willing to finance the company – and has contributed substantial efforts to support a turnaround.
“Had we not, the company would have collapsed into insolvency in August 2025. Our efforts have continuously focused on the company’s value and its people, not prioritising one over the other.”

articles.title: DOJ: Complainants' consent among factors in US extradition request for Quiboloy
articles.summary: An executive from the Department of Justice (DOJ) said that one of the factors being considered in the extradition request of the US for Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) founder Apollo Quiboloy is the…

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 9:45pm

An executive from the Department of Justice (DOJ) said that one of the factors being considered in the extradition request of the US for Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) founder Apollo Quiboloy is the consent of Philippine complainants, but maintained that the process itself was sui generis.

The DOJ has already filed an extradition request for Quiboloy and two of his co-accused to the United States before a Makati court. Asked about what would happen to the local cases faced by Quiboloy, Vasquez explained that they could either be completed before the extradition process or temporarily suspended.
There are several conditions that need to be assessed before an extradition request is granted, according to Vasquez.

“Kasi pending din sa atin. Hindi mo naman pwedeng sabihin na mas importante yung rule of law nila tsaka yung justice system nila doon kasi mayroon ding tao na victimized dito,” Vasquez said in a press briefing.
(Because it is pending with us. You cannot say that their rule of law and justice system is more important there because there are people who are victimized here.)

“Kaya one of the items that would be considered would be, yung sinasabi nilang consent of those private complainants dito sa Pilipinas. But at the end of the day, ito kasing extradition is a sui generis process,” he added.

(So one of the items that would be considered would be. What they call is the consent of those private complainants here in the Philippines. But at the end of the day, this extradition is a sui generis process.)

Suis generis is a legal term describing something as a class of its own. Vasquez said that extradition is not a criminal or civil case, but an administrative judicial proceeding where the degree of proof lang niyan is prima facie.

Vasquez said that the court will have to check if the case satisfies both the extradition treaty and Philippine laws. The court also has to confirm that the subject of the extradition request is the same as the person being presented before the tribunal.
The crime that the US is charging Quiboloy with should also be considered a crime in the Philippines, regardless of the name of the crime.
Quiboloy is wanted in the US on sex trafficking charges, and in the Philippines, he is facing charges of qualified human trafficking and sexual abuse. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: ‘A second chance’: children guilty of serious offences will no longer have to declare criminal records
articles.summary:
Government proposal aims to reduce number of children in custody in England and Wales and boost youth employment

Children found guilty of robbery, dealing drugs to other children or violent…

blocks.text: Children found guilty of robbery, dealing drugs to other children or violent disorder will no longer have to disclose their criminal records to prospective employers under sweeping government proposals to change the youth justice system.

People in England and Wales will not have to share records of crimes committed when they were under 18 for the rest of their lives under the proposals, which ministers say will boost youth employment and make life fairer for people from disadvantaged backgrounds in particular.

The proposals, which are being consulted on, are part of a wider set of changes that aim to sharply reduce the number of children in custody and increase support for those who are convicted of crimes.

Jake Richards, a justice minister, told the Guardian: “Where it’s safe, we believe as a government, people should have second chances – second chances to make something of themselves, to contribute to work and to turn their back on crime.
“The system at the moment doesn’t discern for offences committed when you were a child than those that you committed as an adult.”

Richards is proposing to reduce the number of offences that would require lifelong disclosure on standard and enhanced DBS checks by the person who committed them. If the plans become law, people convicted of violent disorder, supplying drugs to a child, robbery, affray and actual bodily harm when under 18 would no longer automatically have to disclose those offences for the rest of their lives.

If they are convicted of one of those offences but do not get a custodial sentence, they will have to disclose them only for five and a half years. If they get a sentence of two years or less, they would have to disclose it for 11 years.
Anyone given a longer custodial sentence would still have a lifetime obligation to tell prospective employers.
If someone is convicted of a crime which results in a fine, they will no longer have to disclose it, rather than for the next six months as the law currently stipulates.
Jobs in the UK that require a standard or enhanced DBS check include teaching and early years working, social work, healthcare and transport jobs including taxi driving.
after newsletter promotion

Other changes include ending the automatic disclosure of any out of court resolution and ending a rule which lengthens how long it takes for a conviction to become spent if the person is convicted of a second crime during their rehabilitation period.

Campaigners have welcomed the proposed changes, saying they will boost youth employment. Companies say criminal convictions are the second biggest barrier to employing people from disadvantaged backgrounds.

articles.title: China's Xi Jinping renews calls for 'reunification' with Taiwan
articles.summary: Xi Jinping said that reunification was inevitable, but stopped short of mentioning military force. Taiwan though swiftly rejected Beijing's demands as tensions continue over the island's future.

image.caption: Xi Jinping says he wants peaceful reunification but in the past hasn't ruled out the use of forceImage: Ng Han Guan/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: ChinesePresident Xi Jinping has renewed his calls for "reunification” with Taiwanbut refrained from mentioning the use of force.
"The historical trends are unstoppable. The complete reunification of our motherland must be realized, and it can, without doubt, be realized," Xi said on Thursday.

His comments came in a speech marking the 160th birthday of Sun Yat-sen, the political leader who helped lead the 1911 revolution that overthrew China's imperial dynasty and led to the founding the Republic of China.
The Taiwanese government swiftly rebuffed the remarks, saying the territory would not accept submitting to the rule of China's Communist Party.
What is the Taiwan conflict about?
After the founding of the Republic of China in 1912, a civil war broke out in 1927 between the Nationalists and the Communists.
After the end of Japanese occupation and World War II, the Communists led by Mao Zedong gained the upper hand and the Nationalists retreated to the island of Taiwan in 1949.
Since then, both the People's Republic of China on the mainland and the Republic of China in Taiwan claim to be the legitimate heirs of Sun Yat-sen's political legacy.

Under the so-called One China policy, the majority of the international community recognizes only Communist China on the mainland as a state. Many countries nevertheless also maintain unofficial diplomatic, economic and cultural ties with Taiwan, which is self-governed and democratic.
What did Xi say about reunification?
While the speech by the Chinese president was largely about commemorating Sun Yat-sen, it was his remarks about Taiwan that drew international attention.
Xi said that reunification was an unwavering historical mission for the Communist Party and that "we will never leave any room for ‘Taiwan independence' separatist activities in any form.”
"We will definitely give full consideration to Taiwan's realities and take full account of the interests and feelings of our compatriots in Taiwan.
"Mr. Sun Yat-sen consistently upheld the unity of the country and the solidarity of the nation, and he firmly opposed all words and actions that split the country or the nation," he added.
While not mentioning military force in his speech, the Chinese leader has on several occasions in the past said that Beijing would not rule out military force to bring Taiwan under its control.

blocks.caption: China frequently runs military drills in the waters and skies just around TaiwanImage: Taiwan Coast Guard/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: In response to Xi's speech on Thursday, Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council reiterated that neither the government nor the people of Taiwan would accept being placed under Beijing's rule.
"As for the wording on Taiwan unification, it isn't much different from ​the past," council spokesperson Liang Wen-chieh told reporters.
Increased pressure on Taiwan
Xi Jinping's speech came ahead on an APEC summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen where the Chinese leader is expected to meet with US President Donald Trump.
The US has over the past decades been backing Taiwan's resistance against Chinese demands, supplying the island with vital arms support.

China has in past years intensified its military operations around the island and in the Taiwan Strait, widely seen as both attempts to intimidate Taipei and to possibly practice for an eventual military operation.
On Thursday, Taiwan said that Chinese fighter jets and drones had begun carrying out a "joint combat readiness patrol" alongside Chinese warships around the island.

articles.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
articles.summary:
After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’

Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has…
articles.byline: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg and agencies

blocks.text: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.

Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled: “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI,” in which author and journalist Vauhini Vara said AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.

Caine prize chair Ellah Wakatama said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”
She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.

“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”

Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.
Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations they were using AI.
Associated Press contributed to this report

articles.title: Millions of Ebola dollars going missing as virus spreads, medical charity warns
articles.summary: Medical staff are going unpaid, lack proper training and are struggling with shortages of essential supplies, MSF warns

blocks.text: Hundreds of millions of dollars meant to help tackle Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo are not reaching the intended recipients, a medical charity has warned.

Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) says while the outbreak remains "out of control", there is a "considerable disconnect" between what is disbursed and what gets to "patients, frontline workers and communities".
"Despite the vast amounts of money provided for the response, many frontline responders are left trying to contain the outbreak with empty hands and empty pockets," the charity says in a report.
More than 5,400 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.
This makes it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease ever recorded.
MSF has urged the Congolese government and UN agencies to "strengthen oversight and accountability" to ensure money already disbursed is effectively utilised.
This means "ensuring response personnel are properly trained, paid, equipped, and supported, and directing resources towards areas where needs are greatest," it said.

MSF's warning adds to concerns raised by Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) last month, when it said that $700m (£527m) out of $962m disbursed to organisations implementing Ebola response was unaccounted for.
At the time, Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya said it was too early to describe it as embezzlement, characterising the issue as a major transparency and financial reporting failure.
In its report, external, MSF cited "cases of healthcare workers not being paid or trained, ambulances left to run without fuel, a lack of supplies or support for frontline employees".
It also mentioned Ebola monitoring "surveillance teams that exist on paper but are nowhere to be seen on the ground".
"Our teams are often left speechless by the dysfunctions they witness in many areas. Six months into the response, this situation is simply unacceptable," said MSF president Javid Abdelmoneim.

One important way of stopping Ebola from spreading is contact tracing - finding all those people who had come into contact with an infected person and putting them into isolation. "Despite the resources officially allocated to this critical activity, surveillance remains deeply problematic," MSF said, adding that two-thirds of deaths were occurring in communities not treatment centres.
According to British epidemiologist Neil Ferguson, more than half of the cases are going undetected, meaning the outbreak is likely to last another year, reports the Reuters news agency.
MSF also raised concerns over "excessive concentration" of efforts in certain areas at the expense of other areas where needs were more urgent.
It said the response was "too slow" in North Kivu province while Haut-Uélé remained "dramatically overlooked".
In both provinces, MSF observed that teams were "inadequately resourced to respond effectively" with health facilities lacking essential items such as water, chlorine or triage systems.
"This has turned some facilities into new centres of transmission, rather than places of care that contribute to containing the disease," MSF said.

articles.title: Kakampink defense lawyer? Poa says nothing wrong with that
articles.summary: Defense counsel and spokesperson Michael Poa on Thursday addressed the social media posts indicating that one of the lawyers on Vice President Sara"s team for the impeachment trial supposedly…

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 8:59pm

Defense counsel and spokesperson Michael Poa on Thursday addressed the social media posts indicating that one of the lawyers on Vice President Sara’s team for the impeachment trial supposedly supported former Vice President Leni Robredo in the 2022 presidential elections.
In a post-trial press conference, it was brought to Poa’s attention that the Facebook posts of defense counsel Justin Gular endorsing Robredo for president in the 2022 elections had gone viral.
Poa shrugged off the viral post, saying that they only show that Duterte’s lawyers are participating in the impeachment trial as professionals.

“I don't see anything wrong with political affiliations. I don't see how it affects the case. In fact, it just shows that we are professionals and we are doing our jobs as best as we can without any political leanings,” he said.

“What we are here to do is to present the facts and to show that the allegations against the Vice President are baseless. In fact, to us, that strengthens the point, [that] we're not here only because we're politically affiliated or we have political leanings. We're here as professionals, as lawyers, and we're here to present the facts as much as we can for the appreciation of the impeachment court,” he added.
Poa also expressed belief that the viral post would not affect the dynamics within the defense team.

“You know, I don't know who voted for who [in the] defense team, and it has never been an issue. It's not even an issue with the Vice President, so I don't see why it should be an issue between us,” he said.
He also emphasized that his confidence in the defense lawyers remains intact.

“I have full confidence in the team I'm with. We've been working in the trenches for the past two years together, and I have no reason to doubt anyone's capability or even their willingness to help us in this case,” Poa said. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Suspected bomb hoax threats force fresh evacuations of Italian schools
articles.summary: Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.

blocks.text: Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.

Some 1,800 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported receiving a similar threat to one that created chaos in Italy on Wednesday - even though no devices have been found anywhere.
The Italian government has advised schools that "in the absence of concrete evidence beyond the simple receipt of a mass email indicating a danger, buildings must not not be evacuated".
Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threats on Wednesday, too. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.
On Thursday morning, a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed international and national train services in northern France.
The latest incidents follow a series of bomb hoaxes last week against airports and airlines in a number of European countries.
Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.
Wednesday's email threat - sent to 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 Italian state schools - was said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan".
Some officials say it originated in Taiwan.

A similar message sent to Italian schools on Thursday, again signed by Mikhail Andropov, is said to have been sent from the account of a teacher in the Philippines whose account is believed to have been hacked.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has spoken of "a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern".

articles.title: Duterte-Carpio's purchases questioned as SALN shows no cash declaration
articles.summary: The credit card purchases of Atty. Manases Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, raised suspicion because the couple did not declare any cash on hand or in the bank in their Statement of…

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 8:39pm

The credit card purchases of Atty. Manases Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, raised suspicion because the couple did not declare any cash on hand or in the bank in their Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net worth from 2019 to 2025, the House prosecution team said.

Private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa made the position after the presentation of defense witnesses Anel Antero and Chad Parian, who testified on the credit card purchases of Carpio, worth over P200,000.

Antero testified that he partly reimbursed Carpio for the P200,000 meal they ate with a group at Ginza in Tokyo, Japan, while Parian said that Carpio paid for over P256,000 worth of shoes for the children of Elite Basketball team and their parents in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.
The single-transaction credit card purchases were part of the financial forensic report earlier made by accountant-lawyer Alex Cabrera, a witness for the prosecution.

“Kapani-paniwala ba na ang isang tao na wala siyang dineklara na cash on hand or cash in bank pero merong milyon-milyong lumalabas sa bank accounts at kayang bumili, sa isang gastusan, ng P250,000 worth of shoes?” Tolosa said in a press conference.
(Should we believe that a person who did not declare any cash on hand or in bank has millions in bank deposits and could purchase P250,000 worth of shoes in one transaction?)
“Yun lang naman ho yung issue. Hindi naman po sinasabi na huwag mong supportahan yung anak mo sa sports. Wala naman hong sinabing ganyan ang prosecution,” Tolosa added.
(That is the only issue here. The prosecution is not saying that parents should not support their child in sports. We are not saying that.)
Tolosa did not name names, but senator-judge Pia Cayetano called out the prosecution for asking Parian about the P256,000 worth of rubber shoes.

Private prosecutor Rey Robles also asked Parian if such a purchase by Carpio is compliant with the Code of Conduct for Public Officials and Employees, which states that “public officials and employees and their families shall lead modest lives appropriate to their positions and income. They shall not indulge in extravagant or ostentatious display of wealth in any form."
“Prosecution, I’m warning you. I will not hide my disdain. I will not. I cannot,” Cayetano said of Robles’ questioning.

“Is it the prosecution’s intention to make a parent relinquish their parental duty in terms of rearing their child in the manner they feel is the best to promote character, leadership, teamwork just because one of the parents becomes a public official?” Cayetano added.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: AI helped the UK defy expectations – but will Britain’s resilience fizzle out?
articles.summary: Despite John Healey’s defiance, the economy faces threats from a tech slowdown and energy bills this winter

blocks.text: The forecasters were clear when John Healey became chancellor in July: Britain’s resilience to the war in the Middle East would not last. The global economic headwinds were too strong, inflation was beginning to rise and growth would slow to a trickle.

Four months into the job, the economy is continuing to defy expectations after growing by 0.7% in the third quarter – the fastest expansion in two and a half years – leaving the UK as the second-fastest growing G7 economy this year.

On his first day in Downing Street the memo from the Treasury showed the most optimistic City analyst expected 0.3% growth. Most had pencilled in a figure close to zero. Some were warning that the UK could edge towards a recession.
Despite the gloomy outlook households have continued to spend and business investment has powered ahead, fuelled by the rollout of AI.

Underneath the bonnet, growth is being driven by IT and professional services – together contributing about half of the rise in activity. As the central sectors in the AI boom, that is hardly surprising – with analysts at ING suggesting the strength in IT was “very clearly a datacentre story” thanks to the UK’s status as a leading destination in Europe for investment.

Overall, Deutsche Bank estimates that AI-related spending has added about 0.3%-0.4% to GDP growth this year. It is clear to see why Healey is keen to build on the groundwork laid by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, to harness AI amid government efforts to court global business investment.

Meanwhile, household consumption is up by 1.6% so far this year – helped by spending over the warm summer months even as consumers faced a living standards squeeze because the Iran war fuelled a surge in petrol and diesel prices.
However, the fear is that the UK’s initial resilience to the global economic storm emanating from the Middle East will soon fizzle out.
Both of Britain’s recent growth engines face a tougher period ahead.

After the US midterm elections and revelations at Nvidia, the outlook for the AI investment boom is less certain. Financial markets have been rocked in recent weeks amid fears that a bubble in AI stocks could be about to burst. A slowdown in technology investment could hit the UK. Still, the hope is that swelling demand for AI will not evaporate overnight.
after newsletter promotion

For households, however, a tough winter lies ahead. Energy bills are poised to increase by about a quarter in January, with the average annual household gas and electricity bill poised to climb to more than £2,000. Analysts say it is hard to see how consumer spending would not come under greater pressure in the new year.

In the latest data there were some early warning signs: retail sales and consumer discretionary spending fell in September. Real wage growth is cooling and the headline inflation rate is on track to reach a fresh peak of close to 5% next year.

With growth proving resilient, the Bank of England will feel emboldened to raise interest rates to combat imported inflation. City investors expect at least two more quarter-point increases to 4.5% before the end of next year. That will hit the brakes on the economy and add to the cost of living squeeze.
At last month’s budget Healey struck a defiant tone by arguing that the UK could continue to defy forecasters expectations. That task, however, is becoming increasingly tough.

While some senator-judges were frustrated by the “evasive” answers of a defense witness to questions about trips to China, Senator-judge Robin Padilla was puzzled why it was even an issue in the first place.

Padilla expressed his confusion over the matter at the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. on Thursday, November 12. This was days after the first defense witness, Davao City Assessor Jaime Adalin, irked some senator-judges to the point of contempt warnings, after he evaded, then brushed off, the question of prosecutor Jay Tolosa about a China-sponsored trip just the past year.
Like Adalin, Padilla also did not see the relevance of the question. “Bakit po issue ‘yung pagpunta sa China (Is traveling to China an issue)?” Padilla asked the prosecution.
He shared that he had been to China several times, once with former president Rodrigo Duterte, but he could not recall the names of the places that he visited.

“Di ko rin ma-recall saan ako nagpunta kasi di pumapasok sa isip ko po na ‘yung mga lugar sa China siguro di talagang familiar sa akin. At tinanong ko pa staff ko saan ako nagpunta dahil di ko matandaan. Totoo po ‘yan. Problema po ba ‘yun kung di mo matandaan kung saan ka nagpunta sa China?” Padilla asked prosecutor Terry Ridon.

(I also couldn’t recall where I went because it didn’t enter my mind, the places in China are really not familiar to me. And I asked my staff where I went because I couldn’t remember. That’s true. Is that a problem, if you can’t remember where in China you went to?)

Ridon reiterated the prosecution’s response at the Monday hearing that the queries on Adalin’s foreign travels were made to test his credibility as a witness. He also stressed the issue was not Adalin’s travel to China but his failure to give direct answers about the trips.

“‘Yung pagpunta sa China ay bahagi ng pag-test ng credibility ng witness. Walang usapin kung naging maagap ang testigo sa pagsagot ng tanong patungkol sa biyahe sa China. Wala naman sanang debate kung agad-agad inamin mismo…. Ang issue ‘yung parang di pagiging matapat sa harap ng korte,” Ridon said.

(The questions on the trip to China are part of testing the witness’ credibility. There should have been no issue if the witness immediately responded to the question about the trip to China. There would have been no debate if he admitted it immediately…. The issue is that he did not appear to be honest before the court.)

blocks.caption: Padilla to prosecution: ‘Bakit issue ‘yung pagpunta sa China?’

blocks.text: On Monday, Adalin, as Senator-judge Panfilo “Ping” Lacson described it, “almost made a mockery of the court” when he smirked and deemed as “irrelevant” a prosecutor’s question about an alleged all-expenses-paid trip to China in November 2025. After contempt warnings, the Davao City assessor eventually regained his memory and recalled the trip.

At the trial on Thursday, Padilla said witnesses’ responses should be respected, echoing the reminder of Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero at the start of the trial that morning. He called on counsels and the impeachment senator-judges to exercise restraint and give witnesses due consideration when they say they are unable to recall certain details.

Escudero, however, was apparently referring to another witness, Gencorp in-house counsel Suzette Balucanag-Punay, who faced intense grilling from some senator-judges the day before. She had testified that the Vice President received over P2.1 million in “return of capital” from Gencorp between 2022 and 2025 from what she called a “loose investment.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘I had the courage to believe in Mississippi’ says Scott Colom after historic Senate win – US politics live
articles.summary: Colom adds to blue wave of Democrat victories across the US and becomes Mississippi’s first black senator since 1875 after defeating Cindy Hyde-Smith

blocks.text: Key events

items: 9m agoTrump attacks Democrats over ‘blue state corruption’ in Truth Social tirade
40m agoColom makes history with Democratic Senate victory in Mississippi

blocks.text: Trump attacks Democrats over ‘blue state corruption’ in Truth Social tirade

Donald Trump has been busy posting his latest commentary on Truth Social this morning, publishing a series of posts in which he takes aim at Democrats, revisits old grievances and accuses his political opponents of corruption.

In one post, the US president launched an attack on the Democratic party, describing its leadership as “one of the most corrupt and anti-American” in the country’s history. Coming just days after the Republicans suffered significant losses in the midterm elections, Trump’s latest broadside against Democrats appears to be an attempt to rally his party, as he urges Republicans to “fight hard”.
He wrote:

double quotation markThe Democrat Party, lead by one of the most Corrupt and anti-American groups of political leaders and hacks in the history of our Country, and even the World, is doing everything in their power to get away from MASSIVE BLUE STATE CORRUPTION by saying, over and over again, that the Trump Administration is corrupt. It is a sound bite that they viciously use, over and over again, in order to nullify the TREMENDOUS & UNPRECEDENTED theft that has taken place in our Blue States - Minnesota, California, and others, all over the U.S.A.

In a subsequent post, Trump returned to the controversy surrounding his personal tax returns during his first presidential term. He recalled what he described as a “relentless effort” by Democrats to obtain his tax records, claiming that, after the matter reached the Supreme Court, accountants spent a year examining his finances in an effort to find wrongdoing.

Unlike previous presidents in recent decades, Trump refused to voluntarily release his returns while campaigning for the White House and throughout his first term. After a lengthy legal battle, six years of Trump’s tax returns, covering 2015 to 2020, were subsequently made public by the House ways and means committee. You can read more on that here.
On Truth Social, Trump wrote:

double quotation markNow, in order to deflect from MASSIVE BLUE STATE CORRUPTION & CRIME, they are at it again, illegally threatening Republicans with knowingly false accusations and charges. Other than cheating, this is how they won the Midterms - But we won’t let our Country go to hell!
Colom makes history with Democratic Senate victory in Mississippi
Hello, and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Mississippi has elected Scott Colom, a Democrat, as its senator, adding to a wave of Democratic gains across the country in this year’s midterm elections.

He defeated incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in the closely contested Senate race to become the state’s first black senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era, marking a historic moment for Mississippi and a major breakthrough for the Democrats in a traditionally Republican state.

blocks.caption: Senator-elect Scott Colom raises a fist during his victory rally in Tougaloo, Mississippi on Wednesday. Photograph: Lauren Witte/Clarion Ledger/Reuters

blocks.text: “All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this,” Colom said in his victory speech last night.
“I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters.”
Just over a week since the midterm elections, the Associated Press called the race after absentee and provisional ballots were counted.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Hyde-Smith said.
You can read more about Colom’s grassroots campaign, his viral advertising strategy and how he reached voters at Trump rallies despite limited early backing from national Democrats here:
In other news:

blocks.caption: US special envoy Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner and Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev walk from hotel for a scheduled meeting in Moscow, Russia. Photograph: Yulia Morozova/Reuters

articles.title: What are fossil fuels?
articles.summary: They are in our shampoo bottles, power our cars and heat our homes. But what actually are fossil fuels, and why do they matter?

image.caption: Fossil fuels such as coal can be found hundreds of meters below groundImage: Omer Urer/AA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Whether in the form of crumbly rock, odorless gas or slick black liquid, ancient organic compounds have powered the flourishing of modern life. But now they threaten to make the planet unlivable for many plants, animals and humans.
What exactly are fossil fuels?
The collective term refers to coal, oil and natural gas — a group of energy sources that contain carbon and hydrogen.
They started life hundreds of millions of years ago as living plants and animals. When they died, they sank to the bottom of oceans and swamps where they decomposed under layers of sediment.

Over time, this matter was buried deeper and deeper into the earth, subjecting it to increasing pressure and heat which changed its chemical composition. Plants and trees transformed into coal, whereas microscopic plankton and algae became oil and — if the heat and pressure increased further — gas.
Today fossil fuels can be found in the earth's crust all around the world although some countries, such as the US, Saudi Arabia and Russia, have bigger reserves than others.
Coal, found in underground coal beds, is extracted by mining, whereas oil and gas, found in reservoirs beneath the land and ocean, are accessed by drilling.
How countries are skipping 200 years of carbon emissions
How are fossil fuels used?
Since the early 19th Century, when the discovery and exploitation of fossil fuel reserves powered the Industrial Revolution, our use of them has skyrocketed, increasing eight-fold since 1950.
Today they provide 80% of our energy needs through heating, electricity generation and transport.

We transform them into energy either by burning them directly in furnaces that warm up our homes and businesses, or in power plants to heat water into steam which then generates electricity. When it comes to transport, crude oil is refined into a range of products such as diesel, gasoline and kerosene that are burned in the engines of automobiles, airplanes and ships. Natural gas is also sometimes compressed for use in cars and buses.

But fossil fuels are also essential to a huge range of products including steel, formed using a coal-derived material called coke, and plastic, which is produced by refining and processing crude oil and gas.
What is the future of fossil fuels?

Fossil fuels are by far the biggest contributors to climate change. When burned to power our modern lives, they emit carbon dioxide (CO2) into Earth's atmosphere, trapping heat and causing temperatures to rise.

blocks.caption: The pollution from burning fossil fuels causes millions of premature deaths every yearImage: Vuk Valcic/ZUMAPRESS.com/picture alliance

blocks.text: With 2025 officially one of the warmest years on record, the impact of these emissions is being felt around the world. Hotter temperatures are causing polar ice caps to melt and creating the conditions for extreme weather events — such as floods, drought, wildfires and storms — to become more intense and frequent.

Scientists stress the need to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to avoid unleashing the most catastrophic impacts of climate change. That was laid out in the 2015 Paris Agreement. Currently, there are 194 parties to the agreement, but progress has been too slow, and overall emissions continue to rise.

Three years after countries agreed at the UN climate conference in Dubai COP28 to transition away from coal, oil and gas. After the previous COP in Brazil failed to reach a consensus on a concrete plan, Brazil has now presented a roadmap aimed at turning that promise into national plans.
"It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable," United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said.

articles.title: Paolo Duterte seeks Matibag inhibition from probe into Gracioso allegations
articles.summary: Davao City Rep. Paolo Duterte has asked the NBI and its director Melvin Matibag to recuse themselves from investigating allegations made by Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 7:58pm

Davao City Representative Paolo Duterte has asked the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) and its director Melvin Matibag to recuse themselves from investigating allegations made by Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., according to the agency.

Based on the November 10 letter obtained by GMA News’ John Consulta, Duterte’s lawyers asked NBI’s and Matibag’s office for their "voluntary inhibition from the ongoing investigation,” citing three grounds.

“First, the NBI and your office have already taken an ante litem public position on the veracity and truth of the allegations of Mr. Gracioso…Second, our client has been denied a fair chance to be heard.

“Third, your prior public engagement against the Vice President [Sara Duterte] gives rise to a reasonable perception of bias, worse deliberate effort to trash and destroy her unsullied good character and reputation,” they said.
Matibag rejected the request, saying it had no legal basis.
In a statement on Thursday, Matibag said the concept of inhibition and "cold neutrality" invoked by the congressman’s counsel applies to those tasked with making judgments, not to investigators.
"The NBI does not judge. It establishes facts," Matibag said. "The law gives the Bureau the authority to investigate, and no law requires it to set that authority aside."

He said determining probable cause is the responsibility of the prosecutor or the Office of the Ombudsman, adding that Duterte would have the opportunity to answer the allegations if the matter reaches that stage.

Gracioso, an ex-security aide to former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco, claimed that he delivered suitcases containing over P2 billion in cash to Sara, Paolo and their father, former President Rodrigo Duterte.
Paolo’s lawyers also said the NBI did not furnish them a copy of Gracioso’s affidavit before it was publicized on September 25.
Matibag maintained that Paolo had not been deprived of his rights, saying the lawmaker received Gracioso's affidavit on October 5 and that the NBI's invitation for him to give his side remained open.
The formal opportunity to answer the evidence would come during the preliminary investigation, he added.
Regarding his three columns against Paolo’s sister Vice President Sara Duterte, Matibag said these were written in 2024 before he became an NBI director. — BM, GMA News
