articles.title: Where the US's war with Iran stands after the midterms
articles.summary: Almost nine months after it began, the war in Iran has calmed to the point where Donald Trump sees an end. But with the key issues of the conflict unresolved and political change in the US, what is…

image.caption: Donald Trump endured a difficult midterm loss, with Iran a key issueImage: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The US-Israel war with Iran, according to US President Donald Trump, "is effectively over" in a military sense. Trump's secretary of state, Marco Rubio, backed up the president, saying there is "no need for major combat operations" in Iran because economic pressure and negotiations between the warring parties are proving effective.

However, Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary, Mohsen Rezaei, has denied negotiations are even taking place. "All American claims about the continuation of negotiations with Iran are aimed at easing economic pressures and reducing oil prices," he told Lebanese channel Al Mayadeen.
Is the Iran war actually over?

While neither side has claimed the conflict is concluded in every sense, Ian Kelly, a former US ambassador who now works at Northwestern University in the US, considers the current situation is something like a "virtual ceasefire." He added that there is currently a significant deescalation but that the central issues are unresolved.

"I wouldn't say the war is over. I would say there's no shooting going on, nothing really significant," Kelly told DW. "But the real issue is opening up the Strait of Hormuz. What Iran wants, of course, is for the United States to withdraw its massive strike forces from the Gulf. But that won't happen until Iran agrees to open the Strait of Hormuz."

A critical shipping lane between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, the Strait of Hormuz has been a focal point in the US-Iran conflict. Iran's attacks on commercial ships in the strait have led to higher oil prices and have had other economic impacts that have affected living costs in the US and around the world.

Kelly, who also held several high-level roles at the US State Department, thinks the US midterm election results, which will see the Democrats take control of the House and Senate next year after catastrophic losses for Trump's Republicans, means Iran is sitting tight.

"I think that Iran is in a wait-and-see moment to see if the war will wind down because Congress acts to either cut off the funding or severely limit the funding," he said. But with Iran's resources also dwindling, it's a game of cat and mouse.
What has this conflict meant for Donald Trump and what's next for the US?
Trump and his party need the war to end, according to Kelly, for political reasons, as well as strategic.
"As long as the war is not resolved, it's going to be a real sticking point for the Republicans as they look at [the election in] 2028. They have to wrap it up before then," he said.

"A major contributing factor to the Republican defeat was how Trump has not followed through on some of his promises made in 2024. One of the big ones was no more forever wars, and he just went off and started another war that doesn't seem to have an exit strategy. It has weakened the Republican Party."
Trump weakened: Is Europe safer now?
The imminent change in US politics will naturally have military consequences long before the 2028 election.

”There is little likelihood that Congress will continue to fund this war at the kind of levels that they have been," said Kelly. "That's another reason that Iran is sitting back and just waiting to see where this all comes out."
What needs to happen for a compromise to be reached?

While the US administration claims it is happy with a status quo of containment through land and sea blockades, Kelly believes the authority of Trump and his party will be further diminished if the US can't achieve concrete progress on its stated main goals: gaining full control of the Strait of Hormuz and forcing Iran to give up its enriched uranium.
"Both of those are quite possible," Kelly said, adding that even attempting to achieve them threatens the current relative calm.

"The White House has really painted itself in a corner here by stressing that the main goal is to deny Iran a nuclear weapon. I don't see that as something that Iran is going to negotiate away, which means that they [the US] will probably have to use military force again. The White House is in a real pickle."
But there is also the question of how long Iran can bear the economic burden of the war without reaching a deal.

"Iran's limitation in the Strait of Hormuz is economic rather than military, because continuing the war has a significant impact on its economy," Ali Mohammadi, an expert in Iranian affairs based in France, told DW earlier this week.
Nevertheless, the strait remains a key source of leverage for Iran in any future negotiations.
What would the end of the Iran War mean for the world economy?
Kelly doesn't see the economic strain of the war subsiding anytime soon, especially in oil markets.

blocks.caption: The Strait of Hormuz remains key to bothe Iran and the USImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: "The real issue for the markets is that as long as it remains a phony war, it's very difficult to see oil prices lowering. The prices that are being charged now factor in the possible return to instability, so it has to be some kind of agreement where all sides and the oil markets are confident that we see a return to status quo. It's going to be difficult to restore the markets' confidence that these tankers won't be shot at again," Kelly said.

Given the global consequences of the conflict, Kelly expects it to be a hot topic at this month's APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation) summit in Shenzhen, where Trump and his counterparts in Russia and China, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, will reportedly meet.

"I think Russia is interested in keeping the United States tied down like this. China, though, is interested in resolving it because they are a big customer," he said. A G20 summit in Miami follows the APEC meeting in December.

While the impasse between Iran and the US shows little sign of being broken, the fighting has calmed, for now at least. What happens in the coming weeks in the meeting rooms of Shenzhen and Miami currently looks more critical to finding a solution than what happens on Iranian territory or waterways.

articles.title: Chiz cautions senator-judges against harsh questioning of witnesses
articles.summary: "An answer which may be unsatisfactory is not inherently contemptible."

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 1:35pm
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian (left) and Senate Impeachment Presiding Officer Francis Escudero (right) at the Senate impeachment court on Nov. 12, 2026.
Senate PRIB
MANILA, Philippines — After tense exchanges at the Senate impeachment court, presiding officer Chiz Escudero reminded senator-judges and lawyers to exercise restraint in questioning witnesses.
Escudero said witnesses in Vice President Sara Duterte's trial are entitled to protection from insulting questions and harsh treatment, even when their answers are unsatisfactory.
"The chair wishes to emphasize that an answer which may be unsatisfactory is not inherently contemptible," Escudero said.
He cited Section 3, Rule 132 of the Rules on Evidence, which outlines the rights and obligations of witnesses during judicial proceedings.
"A witness must answer questions, although his answer may tend to establish a claim against him," Escudero said, quoting the provision.
The rule also protects witnesses from irrelevant, improper or insulting questions, as well as harsh or insulting behavior during examination.
It further limits questioning to matters pertinent to the case and provides protections against self-incrimination and questions that could unfairly damage a witness's reputation.
Chiz acknowledges own impatience

Escudero acknowledged that he, too, had shown frustration during earlier proceedings, when defense witnesses struggled to answer questions about properties linked to Duterte's Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).

"The chair wishes to remind the members of this court as well, including the presiding officer himself, who stated that his patience was wearing thin the other day, that we are sitting as senator-judges in a trial," he said.

During Tuesday's hearing, Escudero told Davao City accountant Vingelin Bajan that his patience was running out after she repeatedly struggled to recall details of her former partnership in an accounting firm that audited companies linked to Duterte.
Other senator-judges also questioned Bajan's recollection, particularly her difficulty confirming documents and transactions involving the firm.

The previous day, Davao City Assessor Jaime Adalin faced similar scrutiny over his inconsistent testimony about properties declared in Duterte's SALN and his inability to recall details of his overseas travels.

The witnesses were presented by the defense under Article II of the Articles of Impeachment, which covers allegations of ill-gotten wealth and failure to fully disclose Duterte's assets and liabilities.

Escudero's reminder came as the impeachment court continued hearing testimony on those allegations, underscoring the obligation of senator-judges to ensure fair treatment of witnesses while examining the evidence before them.

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV returns to Peru to a big welcome, calls it his 'homeland'
articles.summary: An estimated 3 million people greeted Pope Leo XIV in Lima as the Peruvian-citizen pontiff began a six-day homecoming visit to the country where he spent two decades as a missionary and bishop.

image.caption: Pope Leo XIV holds Peruvian citizenship and called the country home for over two decadesImage: Simone Risoluti/Vatican Media/AFP

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV opened the Peruvian leg of his South America tour on Wednesday, telling crowds in Lima that returning to the country where he served for two decades felt like coming home.
The Vatican estimated that about 3 million people lined his motorcade route, the Associated Press reported.
What did he say?
Leo holds Peruvian citizenship and spent more than two decades in Peru as a missionary priest and later as bishop of the northern city of Chiclayo before becoming pope.
Also a US citizen, he is the first pope from either the United States or Peru.
He sang Peru's national anthem with President Keiko Fujimori at the presidential palace.
"Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you," he said, adding that he was "also returning to my homeland."
Leo urged Peruvians to "cultivate honesty, integrity," and to accept that "no one has all the answers."

blocks.caption: As bishop, Leo XIV, then Robert Prevost, had repeatedly criticized Fujimori’s late father, former President Alberto FujimoriImage: Luis Acosta/AFP

blocks.text: He also called for stronger disaster prevention in a country regularly hit by El Nino-linked floods and landslides.
Fujimori said Peru must face the “unfinished task” of reconciliation after decades of insurgent violence, state abuses and sharp political divisions.
What is happening in Peru?
The welcome comes as many Peruvians are weary of their leaders.
The country has had nine presidents since July 2016, and homicide rates have nearly doubled in five years.
Political science professor Alonso Cardenas told AP he sees "no sign of a reaction, no strategy" from Fujimori's government.

blocks.caption: Peru remains a majority Catholic country, making up about 67% of the populationImage: Anthony Nino De Guzman/AFP

blocks.text: Notably, the Catholic Church is more credible than any other Peruvian institution, theology professor Veronique Lecaros told AP, even as Pew data show Catholics falling from 76% of the population to about 67%.

Leo's six-day stay includes a trip to 3,700 meters (about 12,140 feet), considered risky after Leo had part of a lung removed in mid-October because of a malignant tumor. He is due back at the Vatican on November 17.
Pope Leo starts jam-packed South America tour just weeks after surgery

articles.title: Greta Thunberg joins opposition to Pax Silica ahead of Philippines' signing
articles.summary: The Philippines is expected to sign the Pax Silica framework before the end of 2026, though not during the ASEAN Summit.

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 12:35pm
Swedish activist Greta Thunberg speaks to the media as she arrives at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, on Nov. 10, 2026.
AFP / Ozan Kose

MANILA, Philippines — Renowned Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg has joined calls to reject Pax Silica, a US-led initiative to secure global semiconductor and artificial intelligence supply chains.
"Labor, land, and minerals should serve the people and the planet, not fuel the wars and ambitions of imperialist powers," Thunberg said in a social media video posted Wednesday, November 11.
As the Philippines moves toward joining the agreement later this year, Thunberg appeared alongside climate activists and organizers Mitzi Jonelle Tan, Mikaela Loach, Adrian Bonifacio and Kim Saira.
The activists also expressed support for protests against US President Donald Trump's upcoming visit to the Philippines.
Trump is expected to arrive in Manila for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit, with protests planned for Tuesday, November 17.
Although the Philippines is not expected to sign the Pax Silica framework agreement during the summit, the country's Board of Investments expects the signing to take place before the end of 2026.

Drawing opposition. Under the proposed framework, the Philippines has put forward plans for a 4,000-acre industrial center within the Luzon Economic Corridor to support advanced electronics manufacturing.

The project would begin with a 1,620-hectare hub in New Clark City, Tarlac, where development has faced controversy over alleged possible environmental degradation and the displacement of farming and fishing communities.
The Philippines' hub would be the first site developed among members of the Pax Silica consortium.

articles.title: Alleged hacks hit at most 20 government agencies – CICC
articles.summary: Only 10 government agencies have so far filed personal data breach notifications with the National Privacy Commission.

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 12:20pm
CICC says investigators are checking whether some purportedly stolen data are old leaks being recycled.
LagartoFilm / GettyImages via Canva

MANILA, Philippines — Hackers have claimed breaches of around 20 government agencies, about twice the number that have formally reported data incidents to the privacy regulator, the head of the government’s cybercrime coordinating body said.
Investigators are also checking whether some of the supposedly stolen data are "old exploits" passed off as new.

Renato Paraiso, executive director of the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC), said in a radio interview that the 20 agencies hit by breaches are based on alleged hacks whose authors posted purported data as proof.

"Based on the various alleged hacks and incidents — along with the alleged information they claim to have obtained, which is being presented as evidence — there are quite a number of them; around 20," Paraiso said in Filipino on dzBB Super Radyo.

The official tally of 10, meanwhile, came from government agencies that believed citizens' personal information had been compromised, which legally requires them to notify the National Privacy Commission (NPC).

The NPC said on Tuesday, November 10, it had received breach notifications from the Bureau of Internal Revenue, the Securities and Exchange Commission, the DICT, the Presidential Commission on Good Government, the Department of Labor and Employment, PAGCOR, the Department of Justice, the Philippine Coast Guard, the Department of Trade and Industry and Phivolcs.

The vulnerabilities exposed by the breaches in the BIR and SEC have "not just been contained but also remediated," Paraiso said, adding that investigators are still trying to identify the real identities of those responsible for the hacks.

Paraiso confirmed that some data had appeared to be stolen but said investigators were looking at several aspects: whether the datasets were new or “just being recycled to make it look like they hacked our government."
They are also reviewing whether the breaches involve personal information, as in the BIR and SEC cases, he added.
The CICC head said they stepped in because the incidents had risen to the level of cybercrime, and was working with other agencies to identify the people behind the groups.

articles.title: Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital kills at least six, Gaza civil defence agency says
articles.summary: The strike hit the surgery department of the hospital in Khan Younis, wounding at least 20 people and causing extensive damage, a spokesperson says.

blocks.text: At least six people have been killed after an Israeli airstrike hit a building at Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza, an official from the Hamas-run civil defence agency has said.
The strike hit the surgery department of the hospital in Khan Younis, wounding at least 20 people and causing extensive damage, spokesperson Mahmoud Basal told news agency AFP.
A surgeon is reported to be among those who were killed during the strike early on Thursday.
There has been no immediate response from the Israeli military. The BBC has contacted the Israel Defense Forces for comment.
The BBC is prevented by Israel from reporting independently from inside the Gaza Strip, and is unable to verify details of the incident.

Recovery work is carried out by the Civil Defence in Gaza, which operates under the Hamas-run interior ministry. Its efforts have been supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
Nasser Hospital, the largest in southern Gaza, was hit by a double Israeli strike in August 2025, which killed at least 20 people, including journalists and health workers.

Israeli strikes on Gaza have continued despite a ceasefire agreement in October last year. More than 1,600 people have been killed since then, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel and Hamas have accused each other of violating the ceasefire.
The humanitarian crisis in Gaza has also worsened from recent heavy rains that reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents that were housing displaced families.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,645 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title: ASEAN Summit: Metro Manila road closures, alternate routes, traffic advisories
articles.summary: (Updated) What commuters and travelers need to know for ASEAN Summit

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 11:10am

MANILA, Philippines (Updated Nov. 12; First published Oct. 29, 2026.) — Motorists, commuters and air travelers should prepare for road closures, traffic restrictions and possible flight disruptions as Metro Manila hosts the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit in November.
The summit will run from Nov. 16 to 18 at several venues across the capital, primarily the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City.
Security preparations will affect road access around the venue and may also lead to changes in airport operations.
Special non-working days: Nov. 16 to 18

Malacañang has declared Nov. 16 to 18 special non-working days throughout Metro Manila. This is when the ASEAN Leaders Summit will take place. U.S. President Donald Trump is among the leaders expected to attend the meetings.
Under Proclamation 1447, the work suspension is intended to ease traffic congestion and allow authorities to secure areas used by summit participants.
Road restrictions

The Metropolitan Manila Development Authority explained on Wednesday, November 11, that there will be no widespread road closures during the summit, with restrictions limited to designated security zones around the Philippine International Convention Center and Cultural Center of the Philippines Complex in Pasay City.
However, motorists should prepare for temporary traffic stoppages along major thoroughfares whenever convoys carrying foreign leaders and delegations pass through.

MMDA Chairman Romando Artes warned that traffic could be particularly heavy from November 12 to 14 because of convoy rehearsals, traffic simulations, road repairs and adjustments to barriers ahead of the summit.
Access to four streets within the PICC and CCP security exclusion zone is restricted from November 9 to 18, according to the MMDA.
These are:

items: Atang Dela Rama Street
Vicente Sotto Street
Pedro Bukaneg Street
Magdalena Jalandoni Street

blocks.text: Only accredited personnel and vehicles bearing authorized ASEAN stickers will be allowed inside the restricted perimeter. Government vehicles without proper authorization will also be denied entry.
The MMDA said other major roads will remain open, although motorists should expect delays and temporary traffic restrictions during the movement of official convoys.
Authorities have also advised motorists to avoid Macapagal Boulevard, the World Trade Center area, Diokno Boulevard and portions of Roxas Boulevard because of anticipated traffic congestion.
The MMDA said access restrictions around the PICC will be implemented in two phases.
MMDA
Alternate routes and traffic adjustments
The MMDA has designated alternate routes for vehicles traveling near the PICC and CCP Complex.
Southbound motorists traveling along Roxas Boulevard toward Diokno Boulevard and Macapagal Boulevard may take the following route:

items: Turn right onto EDSA.
Turn right onto Diokno Boulevard.
Turn right onto Macapagal Boulevard.

blocks.text: Northbound motorists traveling along Diokno Boulevard and Macapagal Boulevard toward Roxas Boulevard may take:

items: Turn right onto Seaside Boulevard.
Turn right onto Macapagal Boulevard.
Turn left onto EDSA.
Turn left onto Roxas Boulevard.

blocks.text: The MMDA will also implement a stop-and-go traffic scheme along roads used by official convoys. Traffic will be temporarily halted when heads of state and their delegations pass, then allowed to resume afterward.
Artes said these interruptions would generally last only a few minutes.
Truck operators will also be required to follow designated routes from Nov. 15 to 18 to keep container trucks away from Roxas Boulevard.
The alternative truck routes cover roads connecting Manila's Port Area, North Harbor, North Diversion Road and President Osmeña Highway.
EDSA bus lanes, number coding
Designated EDSA bus lanes will be shared with official summit convoys to facilitate the movement of foreign delegates.

The Department of Transportation said buses will continue using the lanes, while traffic personnel will manage their movement to accommodate diplomatic convoys. Private motorists may continue using the regular EDSA lanes.
Motorists approaching the Magallanes Flyover from the Ayala Tunnel should also expect temporary traffic stoppages.
Meanwhile, the MMDA has suspended the number coding scheme from Monday, November 16, to Wednesday, November 18.
The MMDA said it will deploy 2,637 personnel to assist with traffic management and security operations, including emergency response teams and towing personnel.
Motorists and commuters are advised to allow additional travel time, follow posted traffic instructions and monitor official MMDA advisories for further adjustments.

For air travelers: More than 300 flights scheduled between Nov. 13 and 19 have been affected by cancelations or rescheduling. Read Philstar.com's list of affected flights. — with a report from John Marwin Elao

articles.title: Philippines faces difficult mix of high inflation, sluggish growth — BSP
articles.summary: The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas is focusing on the “second-round effects” of global supply shocks and the risk of eroding public trust as the country faces “a difficult…

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 11:07am
Fresh vegetables are displayed at a market in Quezon City on March 4, 2026.
Michael Varcas / The Philippine STAR

MANILA, Philippines — The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas is focusing on the “second-round effects” of global supply shocks and the risk of eroding public trust as the country faces “a difficult combination” of rising inflation and sluggish growth.

The BSP said on Wednesday, November 12, that it is also considering weak aggregate demand as it works to bring inflation down. It added that restoring price stability and purchasing power is crucial to rebuilding public confidence in the central bank and the economy.

"Signs of improvement would include easing inflation, more stable inflation expectations, stronger business and consumer confidence, and a recovery in investment and employment," the central bank said.

Intending to bring inflation back to its 3% target by 2028, the BSP has raised its benchmark interest rate by 125 basis points in 2026 alone, with a "jumbo" 50-basis-point hike implemented in October.
Inflation for the same month was recorded at a three-year high of 7.8%, driven by high energy and transport costs. Economic growth, meanwhile, weakened to 2.1% in the third quarter of 2026.
The BSP will convene for its final Monetary Board meeting on December 17 and release its last monetary policy report on December 23.

articles.title: Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems
articles.summary:
Since the US war on Iran began in February, there have been hundreds of oil spills, posing a ‘generational’ threat to wildlife

The vast, dark slicks in the strait of Hormuz are visible from…

blocks.text: The vast, dark slicks in the strait of Hormuz are visible from space. Throughout October, oil tankers were struck by missiles or sea mines in the waterway and spilled crude into the sea. The pollution has spread across the Gulf, contaminating coastlines and threatening to cause lasting damage to marine ecosystems that are home to dolphins, sea turtles and countless species of fish.
Eight months into the war between the US and Iran, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes has become a battlefield and the centre of a growing environmental disaster.

The naval blockade of the strait has made documenting the pollution from on the ground almost impossible. But analysis of satellite images, combined with the testimony of environmental experts and marine biologists, can help build up a picture.

blocks.caption: Before and after satellite images of an oil spill off the coast of UAE in October

blocks.text: Ecosystem at risk

The strait of Hormuz, the only maritime passage between the Gulf and the Arabian Sea, is home to a rich but fragile marine environment including coral reefs, mangrove forests and seagrass meadows that support a wealth of marine life.

It plays a vital role in the circulation of water and nutrients and serves as a migration route for marine mammals. Even in peacetime, its ecosystems have faced mounting pressure from shipping, oil extraction and coastal development.

blocks.caption: Oil washes up on a beach in Umm Al Quwain, UAE, on 24 October. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: Oil can coat birds’ feathers, making it difficult for them to float and find food. It can cover mangrove roots, preventing the trees from absorbing oxygen and potentially killing them.

Bernhard Riegl, a marine biologist at Nova Southeastern University in Florida, who has studied the Gulf for more than 30 years, warned that the war could cause lasting damage to its confined waters, already under severe pressure from the climate crisis.

“Since the Gulf is shallow, and summer is the least windy period of the year, atmospheric heat is rapidly translated into ocean heat. That heat kills corals, algae, fishes. There is no cold, deep water that could mix and buffer this heat,” Riegl said.

“Everybody knows that oil in water is not good. The potential for additional damage is significant. There is no such thing as a ‘clean war’. Not for the unlucky humans that are drawn into it, nor for the unlucky environment in which the conflict takes place.”
Strikes and spills

Since the war began on 28 February, Greenpeace has identified more than 500 instances of oil spills through satellite monitoring across the Gulf, the strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea. The findings include major spills linked to attacks on vessels, as well as others detected around the time of strikes but whose origins could not be confirmed.

“Adding together the daily mapped footprints [of the spills] gives a cumulative total of approximately 20,000 square kilometres – almost the size of Wales,” said Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief.

More than 133 attacks on oil tankers have taken place since the beginning of the conflict, according to Greenpeace. October was the worst month, with more than 30 confirmed or reported attacks in the strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters, according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. The attacks have continued into November.

Among the most polluting of the October attacks was a strike on the supertanker Gem No 2 off the coast of the United Arab Emirates, which left a slick stretching more than 21 miles (35km). A satellite image dated 19 October shows a huge patch of black moving into the clear waters off the coast of Umm Al Quwain.

blocks.caption: The Gem No 2 ablaze at sea

blocks.text: Greenpeace estimates that an attack on a tanker in early June resulted in a slick off the coast of Oman that covered more than 600 sq km (230 sq miles) at its peak. Two Iranian naval vessels hit in March continued leaking oil for months, said Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher with the Dutch peace organisation Pax.
An attack on the Liberian-flagged Minoan Pioneer on 3 August has also been linked to a major slick.

blocks.caption: The Minoan Pioneer off the coast of Muscat, Oman, on 30 October. Photograph: Arnel Hecimovic/The Guardian

blocks.text: Oil pollution has reached several coastlines since the war began. In March, a slick from the Shahid Bagheri was detected near the Hara mangroves. In April, pollution threatened the protected Shidvar Island, home to coral reefs, seabirds and turtles. Oil was also reported washing ashore at Qeshm Island in August, near important fishing grounds and turtle nesting sites.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Before and after images of an oil slick off UAE in October

blocks.text: Satellite imagery also shows slicks near Oman’s Musandam national park and Iran’s Minab River delta, two areas rich in wildlife. Musandam is home to coral reefs and seabird breeding grounds, while the Minab delta has protected mudflats and forests of mangroves.

blocks.caption: A satellite image showing an oil slick spreading off the coast of Kharg Island, a key oil export terminal for Iran, in May. Photograph: Copernicus Sentinel data/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Environmental organisations are continuing to analyse satellite imagery but warn that the full extent of the damage cannot be established without investigations on the ground, which remain extremely difficult. Some of the researchers and environmentalists contacted for comment in Iran and Gulf states said they had been instructed by domestic authorities not to speak publicly about the environmental damage caused by the war.

Establishing responsibility is not straightforward, but Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has been blamed for most of the attacks. US forces have also targeted tankers, disabling Iranian vessels attempting to cross a US naval blockade and striking others in response to Iranian missile attacks on US warships.

According to a Wall Street Journal report, the largest oil spill was caused by a strike carried out by the UAE’s air force on oil storage tanks on Lavan Island. The strikes resulted in crude oil flushing into the Gulf and affecting coastal areas, including the nearby nature reserves of Shidvar Island.
The damage ahead

In some instances, countries bordering the strait have responded to spills. After the attack on the Gem No 2, for instance, the UAE closed beaches, launched a major cleanup and monitored its desalination plants. Authorities said on 30 October that the leak had been stopped and pollution was declining.
In Oman, divers and equipment were deployed to a damaged vessel and crews cleared oil from 7 miles of coastline near the Hallaniyat Islands.

blocks.caption: An oil slick along the southern coast of Qeshm Island, Iran, on 13 August. Photograph: ISNA/AFP/Getty Images
Beaches being closed in UAE after oil spills caused by tanker attacks

blocks.text: But the wider environmental damage may prove far harder to contain. “Oil could remain trapped in sediments, shorelines and mangrove roots long after slicks disappear, damaging marine food chains and threatening coastal communities dependent on fishing,” Noelle said.

Contamination can affect organisms ranging from small invertebrates to fish, birds and turtles. “Mangroves and coral reefs can take decades to recover, particularly when oil persists in sediments,” she added. “Repeated spills, such as those in the strait of Hormuz, risk worsening the damage.”

Riegl said the aftermath of the Iran-Iraq war of the 1980s and the first Gulf war, when tankers, loading facilities and oilfields were targeted, provided evidence of the lasting impact of large-scale oil pollution on Gulf ecosystems.

A 2020 study traced widespread deposits of tar – the thick, sticky residue left as crude oil breaks down – on Qatari beaches to the Gulf war. A study in 2022 found sediment on Saudi Arabia’s Abu Ali Island still contaminated by oil from the 1983-85 Nowruz spills during the Iran-Iraq war, which collectively leaked 80m gallons of crude into the sea.

blocks.caption: Workers clean a stretch of beach after oil washed ashore in Sharjah, UAE, 3 November. Photograph: Altaf Qadri/AP

blocks.text: Riegl said: “Any organism that has to dig into beaches [affected by spills], like sea turtles when they lay eggs, will encounter the contaminated strata and adverse effects can be expected. Burrowing organisms like ghost crabs will continue to bring contaminated material to the surface.
“Clearly, the effects of large-scale oil pollution remain detectable for decades – so this is a generational problem. We could really lose something irreplaceable.”

articles.title: Australian teen missing in bush for six days rescued alive
articles.summary: The 17-year-old's mum has joked that he is "grounded for life" and "never leaving the house again".

blocks.text: A teenager missing for six days in dense Australian bushland has been found alive.
William, whose surname has not been released, disappeared last Friday while on a camping trip with a friend in bushland about 180km (112 miles) east of Melbourne, Victoria.
Extremely cold overnight temperatures had left authorities concerned for the 17-year-old's welfare. Police dogs, divers and helicopters had been involved in the search.
He was located on Friday morning and reunited with his relieved family, who said he was uninjured but "grounded for life".
Rescuers winched William to safety, and fed him a doughnut and a bottle of water, before he was taken to hospital for a check up.
The boy's mother, Elizabeth Barkley, told reporters the teenager had "only a few scratches" and seemed fit and healthy.
"He's doing fine, everything seems to be fine, he's in perfect health," she added.
"He just stayed in one spot and waited to be rescued and I'm just over the moon he's alive."
Joking, she added: "He's never leaving the house again."
Police have said officers were emotional to have found the teen alive.
"It doesn't happen all the time," Victoria Police Acting Inspector Jason Benbow said. "I'm sure he's got a story to tell us soon, which we're very keen to hear," he added.

articles.title: Australian teen who went missing in bushland wearing only shorts and boots found alive after six days
articles.summary:
William, 17, was reported missing after straying from his camp near Walhalla in Victoria’s Gippsland region

  • Get our

blocks.text: A teenage boy has been found alive after disappearing in dense bushland wearing only shorts and work boots nearly a week ago.
Police AirWing found William, 17, whose surname has not been shared, on Thursday morning.
The teenager was reported missing after straying from his camp near Walhalla, 185km east of Melbourne, in Victoria’s Gippsland region last Friday.
He was dropped off by his mother for the weekend to camp with his friend.
It is believed he walked a short distance back to the drop-off location to retrieve further camping equipment.
When he failed to return shortly after, his stepbrother searched the area but found no trace of the teen.
William’s mobile phone, food and water were left behind.
Police said he was last seen near Stoney Creek Road, between Cowwarr and Walhalla on 6 November about 4pm.
On Wednesday, investigators appealed to hunters, campers and landowners to come forward with any information after a hunting camera was found in the search area.
Emergency service workers, including the dog and rescue squad had been searching the dense bushland since last Friday.

articles.title: Hegseth, wife and aides spark scolding from guard at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
articles.summary: A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery issued a verbal reprimand to a group of advisers and staffers with U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth following a…

image.caption: U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth, right, his wife, Jennifer, and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Dan Caine attend a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Va., on Wednesday. (Kylie Cooper/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery issued a verbal reprimand to a group of advisers and staffers with U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth following a Veterans Day ceremony.
Pentagon spokesman said U.S. army sentinel 'correctly and respectfully' called for proper decorum
Video shows Hegseth taking photos on the empty steps in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.
As the group broke from taking photos, a loud laugh could be heard, and the soldier guarding the tomb shouted that "all visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."
Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's top spokesman, said that "while commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."
"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honoured — and will always honour — the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe," he added.
Hegseth delegation appears to be rebuked at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
Incident follows near impeachment of Hegseth

The tomb is considered to be one of the most solemn and revered war memorials in the U.S., being the final resting place of unidentified soldiers from the First and Second World Wars and the Korean War. It has been guarded around the clock — rain or shine — by a soldier from the Army's 3rd Infantry Regiment, also known as "The Old Guard," since 1948.
Hegseth and his staff were at the tomb as part of a larger ceremony commemorating Veterans Day that also was attended by U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice-President JD Vance.
The incident comes a day after Hegseth narrowly survived an effort to impeach him by lawmakers in Congress.

The effort was led by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, and backed by Democrats. However, while Hegseth's critics were not successful in Tuesday's vote, Republicans may have only delayed efforts to impeach him. With Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January, those efforts are likely to be renewed.
Hegseth slammed the effort Tuesday in his first news conference in months, arguing that he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal.
Republicans block impeachment push against Hegseth

A core part of his argument included the assertion that criticisms of him and his handling of the U.S. military were tantamount to an indictment against the nation's service members and their successes.
"On the eve of Veterans Day, these resolutions tell every one of them that their service was a crime," Hegseth said Tuesday.
"This is not patriotism," Hegseth argued. "This is sabotage."
Following the reprimand at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday, the reaction from Democrats was swift.
Rep. Gwen Moore said Hegseth demonstrated "his utter lack of fitness for his office."

"One day after narrowly avoiding impeachment, he shows his contempt for our men and women in uniform by disrespecting the sanctity of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier," she wrote in a social media post.

Pete Hegseth continues to demonstrate his utter lack of fitness for his office. One day after narrowly avoiding impeachment, he shows his contempt for our men and women in uniform by disrespecting the sanctity of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.—RepGwenMoore
It was not the first time members of Trump's team have caused controversy at Arlington National Cemetery.

During his campaign for a second term, Trump attended a ceremony in 2024 to honour U.S. forces killed in the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. A campaign staffer reportedly shoved a cemetery employee trying to prevent two people from filming and photographing the event.
U.S. army confirms Arlington cemetery worker 'pushed aside' by Trump staff

Trump, who had been invited by troops' families, later shared a video on TikTok showing him at the cemetery with a voiceover blaming the Biden administration for the "disaster" of the Afghanistan withdrawal.
U.S. law prohibits campaign or election-related activities within national military cemeteries.

articles.title: Nigeria's president launches re-election manifesto but can he regain voters' trust?
articles.summary: For Nigerians to feel meaningful improvements, reforms will need to go beyond the promises outlined, analysts say.

blocks.text: Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has launched his re-election manifesto, promising to grow the economy, tackle insecurity and address housing shortages.
The plan targets 6% annual economic growth by 2031, 78,000 additional security personnel and 200,000 affordable homes.
Titled From Reform to Prosperity, the manifesto builds on Tinubu's first-term economic reforms, including the removal of the fuel subsidy, which has pushed up living costs.
Nigeria is due to hold a general election in January 2027, with Peter Obi and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar among Tinubu's main challengers.
The manifesto, launched on 10 November by his party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), reflects the government's bid to win back the trust of Nigerians.

Elected in 2023, Tinubu undertook a series of economic reforms, including the removal of fuel subsidies, the harmonisation of official and parallel foreign exchange rates, and tax reforms in Africa's largest oil producer.

"That manifesto was trying to get Nigeria back on its feet, given the condition of the country at that time, slipping into austerity," Joshua Osiyemi, who heads Tracka, a platform launched by the BudgIT Foundation, which is a non-profit organisation that aims to make government financial data easier to understand.
The reforms, although considered necessary by some economists, have been painful for many Nigerians.
"Fuel prices went up, and everything that Nigerians consume skyrocketed," Osiyemi told the BBC.
"Most Nigerian families are saying they cannot survive on 10,000 naira [$7.40; £5.50] a day," he said, referring to a survey conducted by his organisation.

Analysis by Nigeria's International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) found that the price of imported rice rose by 184% between May 2023, when Tinubu took office, and October 2025. Other staples, including beans, garri (cassava flour) and bread, also recorded substantial increases.

In a sign that the reforms might be starting to pay off, SBM Intelligence, a security risk consulting firm, found that the cost of preparing a pot of jollof rice fell by 11.5% between June and September 2026, the sharpest decline it had recorded in the 10 years it has been running its Jollof Index.
However, this has not translated into significant relief for most households.
"Nigerians spend more and more of their income on basics," said Ikenna Okonkwo, head of research at SBM Intelligence.
The reforms were praised by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for their effectiveness.

Nigeria's headline inflation stood at 14% in September 2026, according to the National Bureau of Statistics, down from a high of 34% in 2024. The gap between the official and parallel exchange rates has also narrowed.
Tinubu has said the removal of fuel subsidies freed up more than one trillion ($740m; £550m) naira in government resources in just the first two months.
However, he has recently said he will work to reduce fuel cost.
His administration subsequently announced a 125bn naira intervention package for small businesses, including grants for smaller enterprises and loans for manufacturers.
Atiku has criticised Tinubu's decision to remove the fuel subsidy.
"My position stands! I will restore subsidy to make life easier and affordable for Nigerians," Atiku wrote on X.
However, restoring the fuel subsidy could prove challenging given Nigeria's economic realities.

"The current budget for Nigeria in 2026 is about 68.32tn naira, with 15.8tn going towards debt servicing. So, we are not fiscally strong enough to say that we want to return to the subsidy," Osiyemi said.
While Tinubu's reforms are lauded for restoring some stability at the macroeconomic level, they have also created instability in households.
Two months away from elections, the cost of living and economic hardship are the major issues for many voters.
"These kinds of things can get punished in polls," said Okonkwo of SBM Intelligence.

To address this, Tinubu promised to lower the cost of living, grow the economy by 6% and halve youth unemployment if he wins re-election. Achieving these targets will require increased oil and agricultural production.
But much of Nigeria's agricultural production is concentrated in the north, where insecurity has made farming increasingly difficult.
Osiyemi says many farmers are reluctant to return to their fields.
"They're not sure whether when they go to their farms, they have the chances of also coming back home, to meet with their family."
To address insecurity, Tinubu proposes recruiting an additional 28,000 military personnel and 50,000 police officers.
"The security situation, especially in the north, is more complex than a matter of just recruiting more soldiers," Okonkwo said.
The threats include jihadists, kidnap gangs and conflict between herders and farmers in central Nigeria.

Insecurity is also a major priority for Obi, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate, who came third in the 2023 presidential election and attracted significant support from young Nigerians.
He unveiled his 2027 Governance Agenda on 10 November, under the campaign slogan "A New Nigeria is Possible", placing national unity at the top of his priorities, followed by security.
"Nobody will kidnap school children and disappear into the bush. If you kidnap children and go into the bush, you will not be alone there. We will come after you," he said.

Further, delivering on those ambitions will also depend on improving electricity supply, particularly for businesses and industries. Tinubu promises to increase available electricity generation towards 10,000MW.
"There is nothing in the manifesto about where that investment is going to come from because it will cost a lot of money," said Okonkwo.

Nigeria's power sector has suffered from years of underinvestment. The Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission says the country had installed generation capacity of 13,625MW at the end of 2024, but generated an average of just 4,223MW during the year.
Nigeria's power sector has failed to produce at capacity due to ageing infrastructure, inadequate maintenance, gas supply constraints and funding challenges.

The government has also privatised electricity distribution, but distribution companies have struggled to invest in infrastructure, including local transformers and metering systems, partly because of low profit margins.

"The government cannot increase tariffs to an extent where people will revolt, and that also keeps investors away because they don't look at the Nigerian power sector as somewhere that they can make money," said Okonkwo.
Unreliable electricity supplies force many households and businesses to rely on generators, pushing up the cost of living and doing business.

The manifesto also promises to build 200,000 affordable homes. This is a fraction of Nigeria's estimated housing deficit, which a technical committee set up by the housing ministry put at 14.9 million units in 2025.
For Nigerians to feel a meaningful improvement in their lives, the reforms will need to go beyond the promises outlined in the manifesto, analysts say.
"Some of the items in the manifesto seem bloated, but if they can be committed to it, I want to believe that quite a number of these items that they have here are very much achievable," Osiyemi said.
"The big thing, if the APC wins, which they have to do and is a tall order, is to regain the trust of Nigerians," Okonkwo said.

Nigeria's 2023 presidential election saw Tinubu declared winner with 8.79 million votes, ahead of Atiku and Obi. Tinubu's victory came amid growing economic hardship after eight years of Muhammadu Buhari's APC government.

"APC were able to win because opposition was divided between two very strong candidates with two regional bases. In the end, we still go down to basic questions like the region you are from and tribal sentiments," Okonkwo said.

As Nigeria heads towards the 2027 elections, Tinubu, Atiku and Obi are once again central to the contest, but the opposition faces a familiar challenge: building a united front and support beyond regional strongholds.
"It will play out like it did in 2023," Okonkwo said.
"The APC are in a stronger position being the incumbent party and the momentum that some of the opposition candidates had in 2023 has faded."

articles.title: Nvidia board reportedly weighs ousting Huang amid alleged affairs with exec and suspected Chinese spy
articles.summary: Nvidia's board is reportedly preparing to oust Jensen Huang amid reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The shake-up would leave the world's leading AI chip supplier without the…

image.caption: Huang's potential ouster would leave a leadership vacuum at the roughly $4 trillion chipmaker he cofounded Image: Markus Schreiber/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nvidia's board prepared to oust co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang and could meet imminently to decide his future, media outlets, led by the Wall Street Journal, reported on Wednesday.
Huang has led the company for more than three decades, turning it from a gaming chipmaker into the dominant supplier of chips for artificial intelligence.
Why is Nvidia's board considering replacing Huang?

The report comes as Nvidia investigates whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort after reports of an affair with a woman US intelligence reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him.
News that Nvidia might part ways with Huang sent the company's shares down about 8% in after-hours trading.

A reporter for the financial news outlet Bloomberg said on X that Nvidia's board was working with an outside firm to identify potential successors and considering an interim CEO while it searched for a permanent replacement.
More to come on this developing news

articles.title: 1 dead, 4 critically injured after building collapse in New York City
articles.summary: Firefighters dug through the rubble of a three-story building in Brooklyn on Wednesday after it collapsed at the edge of a construction site, killing at least one person and trapping others beneath…

image.caption: First responders work the scene after a building collapsed in the Brooklyn borough of New York on Wednesday. (Ryan Murphy/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Firefighters dug through the rubble of a three-story building in Brooklyn on Wednesday after it collapsed at the edge of a construction site, killing at least one person and trapping others beneath the wreckage.
Firefighters pulled one person from the rubble of 3-storey building

Firefighters dug through the rubble of a three-storey building in New York City's Brooklyn neighbourhood on Wednesday after it collapsed at the edge of a construction site, killing at least one person and trapping others beneath the wreckage.

Firefighters were called to the scene in the borough's Flatbush section around 4 p.m. News helicopter footage showed dozens of firefighters scouring the debris, with a group homing in on one area and appearing to use a saw to cut through the wreckage.
One person died, and four others were rushed to a hospital in critical condition, according to the New York City Fire Department.
Six additional people were taken to hospitals with minor injuries.
Firefighters search through the rubble on Wednesday. (Ryan Murphy/The Associated Press)
The aerial videos showed firefighters digging at least one person out of the rubble and removing them on a stretcher.

The building that collapsed had been perched at the edge of a lot where another one-storey building had been torn down for a construction project. The site was being excavated, and the building that fell down filled the construction pit with bricks and wood.
Another building that shared a wall with the collapsed structure remained standing, but its wall was shorn off, exposing the rooms inside, including a bedroom and closets filled with clothing.
A wall was shorn off the Brooklyn building, exposing a bedroom and closets filled with clothing inside. (Ryan Murphy/The Associated Press)

A drone hovered over the site as firefighters dug by hand, tossing chunks of rubble aside. Rescuers also used dogs to sniff for survivors. As darkness fell, firefighters used flashlights to illuminate the area where they worked.
Phone and email messages seeking comment were left with the architect, property owner and general contractor listed in city records as being associated with the construction project.

articles.title: Mississippi Senate race: Democrat Scott Colom defeats Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith
articles.summary: The southern US state of Mississippi has elected its first Black senator in more than 140 years. Democrat Scott Colom has won the seat in a historic upset, according to projections.

image.caption: The Associated Press projected Colom would defeat Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith after more than a week of vote counting (FILE: 03/11/2026)Image: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Democratic candidate Scott Colom beat Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's US Senate race after a prolonged ballot-counting process, the Associated Press projected on Wednesday.
The narrow victory makes Colom, 43, the state's first Black US senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction and the first Democratic senator chosen by Mississippi since 1947.
How Colom pulled ahead in Mississippi
During the campaign, Colom promised to represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society.

"It's got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America — a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better," he said.
The southern US state of Mississippi has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations.
Democrats extend their Senate majority

The Mississippi victory gives the Democrats a 55-44 advantage in the 100-member ​Senate. The winner of the Senate race in Alaska remains to be determined. The Democrats also won control of the House of Representatives, having gained 41 seats so far and holding a 254-to-168 advantage, with 13 races yet to be called.
What will Democrats do with their midterm mandate?

Mississippi election officials have been counting ballots for over a week in a race so close that Colom led by only a few dozen votes at some points. The latest media-tabulated results showed him ahead by more than 4,500 votes, or 0.5 ​percentage points.

The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose Republican Party suffered defeats in several states, and it will bolster some Democrats' argument that their future runs through the US South.
Republican rival concedes after close count

Hyde-Smith, 67, posted a concession video on social media, and a spokesperson confirmed she had called Colom to concede. Hyde-Smith was first elected in 2018 and consistently led in opinion polls in a state that ⁠Trump ​won by nearly 23 points in 2024.
Progress or not? Democrats, Republicans pick new leaders in Congress
The Democrats' Senate leader, Chuck Schumer, wrote on X, "Blue Mississippi is here."

Hyde-Smith had blocked Colom's nomination by former President Joe Biden to serve as a US District Court judge in northern Mississippi, citing his position on transgender issues. Mississippi's other US senator, Republican Roger Wicker, supported his nomination for the post.
Mississippi does not have a law mandating a recount for a close election.

articles.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race in surprise victory for party
articles.summary: Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be elected to the US Senate in more than 140 years.

blocks.text: Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, delivering a shock victory for the party in a deeply conservative state that has elected Republicans for decades.
Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be elected to the US Senate in more than 140 years.
Only a few thousand votes separated Colom from his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.
The margin was so close that the race could not be called until more than a week after election day, as local officials counted every single ballot that had arrived before the deadline.
Colon won with 49.2% of the vote, while Hyde-Smith received 48.7% and an independent candidate got 2.1%, according to figures from CBS.
The result means the Democratic majority in the Senate is now 55 seats, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.
It also wipes away a Republican winning streak in Mississippi that dates back to 1982.
The Mississippi contest was never expected to be this close, with Hyde-Smith running for re-election in a state that President Donald Trump won in the 2024 election by more than 22 points.
But Democrats have scored a series of major wins in these midterm elections as the party won control of both the House and the Senate.
It has won Senate seats in numerous Republican strongholds, including Texas, South Carolina and Kansas.
Polls suggest this was due in large part to voter frustrations with the economy and the Iran war under President Trump.

articles.title: Russian Foreign Ministry says its ambassador to US has died
articles.summary: Russia's Foreign Ministry has said that Alexander Darchiev died from a chronic illness at the age of 66. The long-time diplomat had been in the Washington post since early 2025.

image.caption: Alexander Darchiev was appointed ambassador to the US after Donald Trump returned to the White HouseImage: Russian Foreign Ministry/Avalon/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russia's Foreign Ministry said Wednesday that Alexander Darchiev, Moscow's ambassador to the US, died from an unspecified chronic illness in Moscow at the age of 66.

Darchiev was appointed to the post by Russian President Vladimir Putin in March 2025 after Donald Trump returned to the White House and the two countries sought to improve relations. The post had been vacant for six months before his appointment after hardliner Anatoly Antonov was relieved of his duties in October 2024.

In a statement, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova described Darchiev as "an outstanding diplomat, experienced leader, good comrade and mentor" and a brilliant scholar on US history and affairs.
What was Russia's ambassador to US known for?
Zakharova warned against the spread of conspiracy theories surrounding Darchiev's passing, accusing US media outlets of being "particularly active" in that regard.
Darchiev, known for his public denunciations of the West, had previously led the Foreign Ministry's North America and North Atlantic departments and served as ambassador to Canada from 2014 to 2021.
He also led Russia's negotiating team during February 2025 Ukraine peace talks with the US in Istanbul, Turkey.
No date has been given for his funeral.
Details for a memorial service will be announced at a later date, Zakharova said.

articles.title: Two skulls likely belonging to enslaved people returned to Brazil after Harvard used them in eugenics studies
articles.summary:
Remains believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians repatriated after being flown back by diplomats

Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s…
articles.byline: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s greatest slave revolt but whose remains were taken to the United States and used in racist eugenics studies at Harvard University, were repatriated on Wednesday.

The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century. One was taken about 190 years ago from Salvador, the capital of the state of Bahia; the other, about 160 years ago, from Rio de Janeiro – and were welcomed back in moving, subdued ceremonies in both cities.
The skulls are believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians in the country that received more enslaved Africans than any other during the transatlantic slave trade.

Each was brought back in a padded box inside a reinforced suitcase, carried on flights by Brazilian diplomats after a four-year campaign to recover the remains from Harvard’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in the US.
Brazilian researchers from local universities will now try to learn more about who the two individuals were.

blocks.caption: A wood engraving depicting enslaved people being abused on a Brazilian sugar plantation, English, 1845. Photograph: Granger/Historical Picture Archive/Alamy

blocks.text: The skulls will not be displayed in museums or have their images released, and the Brazilian government has pledged that they will be buried with funeral rites as soon as the identification process is complete.

“It’s very important to restore the dignity of these people, which was taken from them in life and in death,” said Carolina Dias dos Reis, a government official who travelled to Boston to sign the agreement with Harvard.

The existence of the skulls was revealed in 2022, and Brazilian researchers sought their repatriation from Harvard, but said they faced a drawn-out process that only moved forward after the Brazilian government became involved in late 2024.
In recent months, concerns grew that Donald Trump’s sometimes hostile behaviour towards his Brazilian counterpart, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, could derail the repatriation. But everything worked out.

“We need to recover our past as a country, however difficult and violent it was, so that we can understand what we are living through in the present: the consequences and scars of structural racism,” added Reis.

Slavery was abolished in 1888, but nearly a century and a half later, Afro-Brazilians make up the majority of the population while occupying the bottom of every socioeconomic indicator, dominating the statistics on hunger, poverty, gender-based violence and victims of homicides committed by criminals or the police.

During the repatriation ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, Ivanir dos Santos, a history professor and a cleric of the Afro-Brazilian religion Candomblé, poured a glass of water on to the ground as researchers received the suitcase.

blocks.caption: One of the boxes containing a skull, at the National Museum in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on Wednesday. Photograph: Ludmila Duarte/MDHC

blocks.text: “It was a ritual act because you cannot deal with the remains of our ancestors without paying reverence to them. This is not a research object … for us, that person is still alive in memory and as our ancestor,” he said.

It is not precisely known who the skulls belonged to. The one taken to Salvador is believed to have belonged to a man who took part in the most significant urban slave revolt in Brazilian history, in 1835, when about 600 African Muslims attempted to seize control of what was then the country’s second most important city. They were ultimately defeated by police, who killed 70 rebels.
The man died at a hospital, and a US diplomat, Gideon T Snow, is believed to have sent the skull to Boston.
The Bahia Islamic Cultural Centre, one of the most active campaigners for its repatriation, has named the man Arakunrin, meaning brother in Yoruba.

Even less is known about the other person: initially, only that they were “an individual … exhumed from the ‘streets of Rio de Janeiro’” in the 1860s. Brazilian government officials, however, said on Wednesday that Harvard researchers had told them that some features – including that the skull was smaller than that of an adult man but larger than that of a child – suggested it may have belonged to a woman.

Bruno Veras, a historian who was part of the group that closely followed the repatriation, cross-referenced diaries, letters and maps of the city and believes the skull may have been taken from a cemetery for newly arrived Africans who either did not survive the long Atlantic crossing or died soon after disembarking.

The person believed to have taken it to the US was Walter Hunnewell, a student from a wealthy Boston family. He was part of an expedition led by the Harvard professor Louis Agassiz, who was in Brazil trying to document physical types to support his racist theories.
“To steal a skull and take it to another country was violent even in the context of racist research,” said Veras.

Researchers in forensic anthropology will now try to confirm the sex of the individuals and other information through measurements of the skulls – the one in Salvador is complete, while the one in Rio is missing its jaw – and microscopic analyses. If necessary, they will seek authorisation to carry out genetic or dating tests.

“This history of slavery cannot be undone,” said Irina Feisthauer Silveira, a diplomat who carried one of the skulls. “But acknowledging the mistakes of the past with transparency is a first step towards building a more equal, just and less violent future.”

articles.title: Hegseth and advisers reprimanded by guard at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
articles.summary: Following a ceremony marking Veterans Day, a group that included Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth was shouted at to be quiet.

blocks.text: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and a group he was with were reprimanded by a sentinel at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday. The incident followed a wreath-laying ceremony marking Veterans Day.

Hegseth had joined the group for a photo and someone laughed, prompting the US Army sentinel guarding the tomb to shout. "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times", the sentinel said.

According to the BBC's US partner, CBS News, the people in the photo before the reprimand also included Hegseth's advisers Patrick Weaver and Tami Radabaugh, Hegseth's chief of staff Ricky Buria and Hegseth's wife Jennifer Hegseth.
"While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum," Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement.

articles.title: Fears of rising antisemitism in Europe
articles.summary: Holocaust survivor Regina Sluszny commemorates the victims of Auschwitz as Jewish communities across Europe face growing hostility. What does the promise of "Never Again" mean for Jewish life in…

image.caption: The infamous line 'Work sets you free' (Arbeit macht frei) is written on the iron gateway to AuschwitzImage: Tessa Walther/DW

blocks.text: Regina Sluszny makes her way in her wheelchair through the iron gate marking the entrance to the former Auschwitz concentration camp. "I feel the cold, both physically and emotionally," says the 87-year-old Jewish woman, her gaze fixed on the grey horizon.

How many times has she been here? Six, seven, perhaps eight, she estimates. And each time, the same thoughts run through her mind: "I think about my husband's family. He lost seven loved ones here. They were sent straight to the gas chambers and murdered."

blocks.caption: Regina Sluszny has spent four decades sharing her story with school childrenImage: Tessa Walther/DW

blocks.text: Regina Sluszny traveled to Poland with a delegation from the European Jewish Association (EJA), a European advocacy group representing Jewish interests that regularly organizes conferences on Jewish life as well as visits to former concentration camps.

This year, the organization invited political representatives and members of Jewish communities to Krakow and Auschwitz on November 9 and 10. The trip was deliberately scheduled to coincide with the anniversary of the November Pogroms of 1938, widely regarded as a watershed moment on the path to the Holocaust.

"Honoring the past, securing the future" is the event's motto. Like many others in attendance, Holocaust survivor Regina Sluszny fears that the horrors of the Shoah are slowly fading from Europe's collective memory.

blocks.caption: A delegation of the European Jewish Association visits the former Auschwitz concentration camp Image: Tessa Walther/DW

blocks.text: Persian-Jewish ties

Among this year's international religious and political representatives, the guest of honor was Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran's last shah and a prominent opponent of the Islamic Republic. The European Jewish Association (EJA) honored him for his efforts to combat antisemitism.
Accepting the award, Pahlavi recalled the historic ties between the Persian and Jewish peoples and called on democratic nations around the world to unite against oppression and ideological extremism.

But talking to attendees at the symposium in Krakow, it quickly becomes clear that fear of rising antisemitism is much closer to home. Many describe growing hostility towards Jews and rising fear in Jewish communities across Europe.
In France, authorities recorded a total of 1,320 antisemitic incidents in 2025. That was fewer than in 2024, but around three times as many as in 2022.

In Germany, the number of antisemitic crimes recorded by police rose from 2,641 in 2022 to 6,236 in 2024 and 6,548 in 2025. Authorities and monitoring organizations across Europe have reported a significant increase in antisemitic incidents since October 7, 2023.

For Ellen van Praagh, chair of the Interprovincial Rabbinate in the Netherlands, October 7, 2023, marked a turning point. She also lost a family member during the Hamas-led attack which saw around 1,200 people in Israel killed and over 250 taken hostage and abducted to the Gaza Strip.

blocks.caption: Around six million Jews were murdered during the HolocaustImage: Tessa Walther/DW

blocks.text: 'We want to live in freedom'

"My family has lived in the Netherlands since the 16th century. And now I'm being told to leave," says van Praagh. She says the atmosphere in the Netherlands has changed dramatically since the attack. She no longer feels safe there as a Jew. "We Jews are being held responsible for Israel's actions."

Israel launched a major military offensive in the Gaza Strip after the October-7 attack. More than 75,000 Palestinians have been killed there since the start of the war, according to conservative estimates.

Like many others at the symposium, van Praagh says she is increasingly losing faith in politicians. "Never Again" has become an empty phrase, she argues, with little relevance to the everyday lives of Jews in Europe.
Jewish communities now have to protect themselves behind high walls. Constant security measures restrict their daily lives, she explains. "That is not what we want. We want to live in freedom."

Rabbi Menachem Margolin, chairman of the European Jewish Association, is also calling on European political leaders to take greater responsibility. He says he is grateful for their support, without which Jewish life in Europe would hardly be possible.

However, laws designed to protect Jewish life are often not enforced in practice. Many officials hesitate to call antisemitism by its name as soon as doing so becomes politically inconvenient. "But Auschwitz did not begin with gas chambers. It began with words," he cautioned.
A visit to Auschwitz-Birkenau — the Holocaust death factory
At the Birkenau memorial

Regina Sluszny joined the delegation visiting the Birkenau memorial. The Auschwitz concentration and extermination camp, built by Nazi Germany, became a symbol of the Holocaust. The Nazis murdered around 1.1 million people there, including approximately one million Jews. Most were killed here at Birkenau.

The delegation is gathered to commemorate the November Pogroms of November 9 and 10, 1938, when Nazis set synagogues on fire, ransacked Jewish businesses and homes and murdered Jews. Around 30,000 Jewish men were deported to concentration camps.

Survivors like Regina are increasingly rare. Most Holocaust survivors have passed away. Regina survived because, in 1942, a family friend and his wife took her in when she was just two years old while her parents fled the Nazis with her two brothers and went into hiding.

For more than 40 years, she has been sharing her story with schoolchildren, doing her part to ensure that the Holocaust is never forgotten. For her, "Never Again" is a promise that must be kept. Otherwise, it becomes a lie.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: African writing award probe finds 'no evidence' winning story was AI generated
articles.summary: Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has also vehemently denied the allegation made in a US magazine.

blocks.text: The Caine Prize for African Writing has said that after an internal review it has found no evidence that Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza had used generative AI to write his winning short story and confirmed him as the winner of this year's £10,000 ($13,000) award.

Ellah Wakatama, chair of the Caine Prize's board of trustees, said the matter had been investigated following an article in US magazine The Atlantic with the headline, Yet Another Literary Prizewinner Seems to Be AI.
"From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human written," she said in a video posted on X.
The accusation had caused a social media uproar and Kundizeza had denied the allegation.
The Atlantic article by journalist Vauhini Vara alleged that AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family falls on hard times was entirely AI generated.

Her allegations followed rows over other literary prizes this year, in particular the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, which was won by Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir despite allegations that he had used AI, and the withdrawal of Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien from France's top literary award, the Goncourt, over allegations he used AI for his first novel, which he denies.
Following the publication of her article last month, Vara had told BBC's Front Row programme that every other previous Caine Prize winning story she had put through Pangram "came out as 100% human".
The backlash on social media included comments from African writers with suggestions that such accusations are primarily being made against non-white writers.

articles.title: Ex-member of radical Marxist group scales balcony, escapes house arrest in Argentina
articles.summary:
74-year-old Leonardo Bertulazzi, awaiting extradition to Italy, reportedly used harness to flee custody

A 74-year-old former member of

blocks.text: A 74-year-old former member of Italy’s radical Marxist group the Red Brigades has escaped from house arrest in Argentina, the country’s security ministry confirmed on Wednesday.
Authorities placed Leonardo Bertulazzi under house arrest in Buenos Aires in 2024, prior to his extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year prison sentence.
He had received the sentence in 1987 for joining a subversive association and belonging to an armed group.

After years on the run, Bertulazzi was first arrested by Argentine authorities in 2002. He was freed a few months later and secured refugee status in 2004, but was arrested again in 2024 after it was revoked.
On Wednesday, Argentina’s security ministry offered a $13,000 reward for information leading to Bertulazzi’s recapture after he slipped out of detention.
The fugitive held a senior position in the Red Brigades, a radical Marxist organization responsible for attacks between 1969 and 1980, dubbed Italy’s “Years of Lead”.
The group most notoriously kidnapped and assassinated former prime minister Aldo Moro in 1978.
Local press went wild describing details of Bertulazzi’s escape from his residence in the capital, but authorities have not confirmed the veracity of any of the reports.
He reportedly used a harness to lower himself from a fifth-floor balcony.
Police noticed his ankle monitor had stopped transmitting movement data and headed to the house, where they found the device discarded and Bertulazzi nowhere to be found.
Argentina approved his extradition to Italy in July 2025 after the country’s supreme court rejected a final appeal.

articles.title: ‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, Marshall Islands president tells Cop31
articles.summary: Hilda Heine warns of effects of catastrophic global heating as world leaders meet in Turkey amid calls for urgent action on fossil fuels
articles.byline: Oliver Milman, Fiona Harvey and Graham Readfearn in Antalya, and Ajit Niranjan

blocks.text: Failure to provide an overwhelming response to the climate crisis means “the world we know is over”, the president of the embattled Marshall Islands has warned, as dozens of leaders gathered in Turkey for the Cop31 climate summit.

Hilda Heine, one of a handful of Pacific Island leaders to make an impassioned speech at Cop31 on Wednesday, told other heads of state that overshooting the 1.5C Paris temperature target would mean waves eating away their shores and floods that destroy towns, schools and hospitals.
